utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-17/1-T, the Prosecutor versus Anto Furundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the accused hear me in a language he understands?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think the parties are as before. Can we proceed with cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honour. Good morning, Dr. Younggren. Your Honour, my microphone is exhibiting red. Am I being heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, I'd like to ask some more questions relating to the Medica institution. There was testimony you gave yesterday concerning inexperience at Medica possibly impacting on Witness A; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had concerns that individuals who are inexperienced trying to treat serious traumatic disorders could actually create problems for patients.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you were concerned also about the institution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had concerns about the goals of the institution being inconsistent potentially with the goals of therapy, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, can I refer you to Defence Exhibit number 25? Dr. Younggren, would you look at the second paragraph on the first page, and the last sentence of the second paragraph, doesn't it read: "The reason why we decided to found the Medica project is that we wanted to assure highly professional help to female victims of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And does the next sentence say: "The help we offer is a combination of medical and psychological treatment provided by highly professional local staff"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, I would like now to have you turn your attention to Defence Exhibit number 22. I would draw your attention, sir, to the bottom of that page where it says, "There is no proven therapeutic concept to help trauma victims who still have to live in life-threatening conditions;" is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Younggren, in your experience, your clinical experience, do people who have PTSD, are they treated in that trauma situation usually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually not. Actually, acute stress disorder patients in combat situations are treated in the setting but Post Traumatic Stress Disorder patients are not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: They're usually removed from the situation, is that what your testimony is, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not really what my testimony is. Individuals who experience combat stress reactions, soldiers, if you will, tend to be treated at the site. That is, they're removed briefly, given some rest and sent back to the units they're involved with, because we have learned that removing them from the situation tends to make the emotional -- long-term emotional reactions more severe. But in Post Traumatic Stress Disorder patients, what you're saying is correct, they are generally treated elsewhere because post traumatic requires four weeks after the event or more, and so generally these people are not in the situation that they're normally exposed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, would you go to the next sentence after the one I read to you before, and doesn't that say, "This means that members of the psycho-team have gradually developed their own concepts for therapeutic practice in war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, to treat post traumatic stress patients in a situation of war, as you've just stated, has its own constraints; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And I would like to turn your attention, therefore, back to document Defence Exhibit D25, the first one, I believe, we looked at, and I would take you to page 2, sir, where it says, "Problem statement." It's at the bottom of page 2. And it states that, "Medica's basic aim is to assist women and girls having been raped and detained in war, as well as to place women to find their psychic balance." Isn't that what it states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, sir, you understand that Medica was treating patients at wartime, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: They were treating patients that could have been diagnosed for post traumatic stress related to that war; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to turn your attention now to D22, and if you would go to -- the pages, unfortunately, aren't numbered, but the third page, sir, and in the middle of the third page there is a headline that says, "Safety In War." Sir, I would direct your attention down to not the first but what would be appear to be the second paragraph after that phrase. It says, "In fact, and particularly, in 1993, 1994, Zenica was under grenade fire;" isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And it says, "The women at Medica panicked every time a grenade struck in the town;" isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, we heard testimony yesterday from Dr. Mujenznovic about Medica, and his testimony, wasn't it, sir, that Medica was a highly respected organisation within the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And wasn't it his testimony also that Medica had staff, such as Dr. Sabic, who were highly regarded among other medical professionals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apparently so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with some of the services that Medica offers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I indicated yesterday, the information that I have about Medica is limited to these materials, because apparently nothing else was available, and so the discussion for me becomes, in some ways, a theoretical discussion addressing these documents, because while I feel strongly that Medica was doing their best, it sounds like it, it doesn't mean that they were doing it right, and the documents also put me in a position of being concerned about whether their goals politically are inconsistent with their treatment goals for patients.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, can I ask a couple of questions, of course based on the documents, as you state you have no other information, about some of the things that Medica did do? Can we turn to D25 again, to the second page, please, and, sir, at the beginning of the second page it talks about organisational profile; doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't see what you're --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, document D25, the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Second page. I'm sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And doesn't it say that it was a women's therapy centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And doesn't it say that it offered gynaecological outpatient services for women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And does it say it had general practitioners, an internist, two anaesthesiologists and six nurses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And two gynaecologists.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Does it talk also about that it had other staff such as -- apart from medical and paramedical, such as administrative staff, a lawyer, a field officer, kindergarten, pre-school teachers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, in that second section does it talk about that it had an ambulance service, meaning a mobile service for its services?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Does it also include a children's programme, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And that's a kindergarten and pre-school service for refugee children; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And in addition to that it talks about psychological care, medical care, that it had a female theologian, psychologist and a sociologist; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, would you consider that a multi-disciplinary service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By definition, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, have you seen anything of these documents that says Medica is a rape crisis centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, have you seen anything in the documents that it says that Medica is a rape crisis centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, would you like to look through the documents to see if it says that Medica is a rape crisis centre?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I interrupt? If it doesn't say so. Just put it rather than wasting time going through the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've just asked the question--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know. Does it say it's a rape crisis centre or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Oh, no, I have not seen anywhere in the documents where it says that. I thought Dr. Younggren might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, Dr. Mujenznovic testified concerning the type of care that Dr. Sabic spoke about at Medica. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And do you remember that he said that Dr. Sabic said that their approach was to gradually come into the subject concerning the trauma that a patient might have? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Madam President, could we ask for counsel to slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- extensive testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, could you slow down for the interpreters, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, yesterday, I believe that you were testifying concerning patients that you treat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I testified that I treat patients who have been exposed to trauma, yes, and also do forensic assessments of trauma victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And you stated, sir, in your testimony yesterday, that you would try to establish the therapeutic relationship and in some gradual and supportive way work through the re-experiencing of trauma. Do you remember that sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I still feel that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: That would be a correct manner of treating someone who had suffered trauma?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a very general sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall that Dr. Sabic also said that the manner of treating trauma -- I'm sorry, not Dr. Sabic. Dr. Mujenznovic, speaking of Dr. Sabic, said the manner of treating trauma was to go in a very slow way to reach the problem, to discuss the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll say again I don't recall that testimony. His testimony was extensive. I'll accept it if you indicate he said it, but I don't recall that, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So you don't have any information concerning their schooling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I indicated, all I have is the material that I indicated earlier. I have no other information. There's nothing available.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, we can't say that that was necessarily an inexperienced psychologist, can we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you have any information concerning any of the academic qualifications or experience of the other people who worked at Medica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only information I have is in these documents, and there is information in these documents that makes me concerned about the techniques they utilised. I don't know specifically about the qualifications of the therapists. I don't even know what the definition of psychologist is, and I wouldn't be able to testify about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, you have no information relating to whether they were inexperienced or not? Yes or no, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't have any information except that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the witness be allowed to finish his answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Except that one of the documents indicates, in Medica's own statement, that they did not know what they were doing when they started to do their work with these victims, and that statement causes me to be very concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, let's talk about these therapies that you're concerned about. You mentioned before that the group therapy might possibly contaminate someone; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, are you concerned about what was mentioned as the dream therapy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what that means, and I'll stay with my testimony yesterday, that that concerns me about dream therapy. Again, it becomes a theoretical concern because I don't know what that means.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir -- pardon me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And it can be potentially risky therapy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, you raised concerns about the imagery therapy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, haven't there been studies done that shows imagery and cognitive interview techniques -- excuse me. Let me stop. Can I ask you, sir, are you familiar with cognitive interview techniques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Among the cognitive interview techniques, isn't there something called "free recall"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Are you familiar that studies done on imagery and cognitive techniques such as free recall have sometime given greater detail to events that have happened during trauma?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that, and also that technique, utilised with individuals who take an active guiding role, has been shown to contaminate memory, so I don't know what they did, but while some studies show that recall is enhanced, it also shows that therapists utilising this technique can create distortions in memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, sir, wasn't that the therapist who used this technique when -- actually, they were blitzing information to children over the period of a year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there are multiple studies, and I'm not sure which one you're making reference to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm making reference to the one from your university by Dr. Giselman and Dr. Fisher, and isn't it true that within their study they found that details and accuracy did come forward with imagery technique and free recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's true and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. And -- pardon me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, there are studies that also show that improperly done, memory can be contaminated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, you testified yesterday concerning your own clinical experience, and your testimony was that after the question was answered, "Do you believe your own patients?" and your response was, "Generally, yes." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So you did qualify that with "unless you get into these extreme areas where I think it's not helpful for people to carry around bizarre belief"; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And I think one of the extreme examples you gave was the satanic cult; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, that was one of two. The other is alien abductions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Alien abductions. That's right, sir. Those are extreme beliefs, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And they would have no context in Southern California; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many of them come from Southern California, but from the scientific perspective, they have no support.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, in a war situation, is it possible that women are raped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not possible, it happens.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you certainly agree that Witness A had horrific events occur to her; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to say it is emotionally upsetting to read what happened to her.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So in the context of Medica in Zenica, a woman who was raped and detained, that's not a bizarre incident, is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And like you would do in Southern California when a patient came, you would probably believe or accept that that person believed what they were telling you; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From a treatment perspective, yes, absolutely, because it's very important to be supportive of your patients. They feel alone and damaged, and the whole sense of having an alliance with somebody who cares and is going to walk through this with you is most helpful, so believing them from an emotional perspective is helpful therapeutically.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, you discussed yesterday when there can be that conflict between the forensic role and the therapeutic role; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I believe that you said that that conflict could be an ethical violation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it can lead to ethical conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. You're someone who testified yesterday that you're fairly familiar with ethical violations as they are pertain to California and the United States, and I'll qualify that for the Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have spent twenty years dealing with them, so I'm fairly familiar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But, sir, isn't that conflict when -- isn't that conflict centred on when the same therapist is the forensic therapist and the treating therapist; isn't that the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. The majority of the articles address that, and I will extend it to organisations only out of my concern that the goals of an organisation may put pressure on a therapist to accomplish certain ends that may not be in the best interest of the patient. I'm not going to leap out and say that Medica is unethical, but I do worry that their goals may not be psychologically helpful for Witness A if this is a part of those goals, and I don't know that. I mean, I'm concerned about the e-mail -- I don't know if I can talk --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It isn't part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: But, Dr. Younggren, you do agree that some institutions can have that dual function but it can't be the same therapist having that dual function; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, and they need to be most careful not to put pressure on the therapist to accomplish those goals.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Sir, for example, you could have a state hospital in California, let's say a psychiatric hospital, that is treating patients, and then -- a psychologist or psychiatrist who are treating patients, but yet that same state hospital could have a reporting function to the California court system concerning that patient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, and generally that reporting function is separate from the treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So an institution can have those dual functions but they shouldn't be mixed in one therapist; is that what you're saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that they should not pressure the therapist to try to accomplish the political/social/forensic goal that could be inconsistent with the treatment goal. So it is possible to do that, and I'm sure organisations do, but I also am sure that organisations don't. But it is possible to separate those, and your point is correct, that they can have those mixed roles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, I would like to turn your attention back again to D25, and this would be on the third page. I don't know whether you have numbers there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. Let me ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I don't. Where it says "Goals and Objectives," and, Dr. Younggren, doesn't it state that "The main goals of our projects are: 1. To provide gynaecological, general medical treatment to women and girls who have been war-raped, detained, and held in home custody or displaced"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Doesn't it say, "The goals and objectives are -- to provide psychological/psychiatric treatment"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And it does say that, among the goals and objectives, "To organise a shelter for refugee women during war. Afterwards, in peace time, the centre could be transformed into a shelter for raped women and girls, if necessary"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And does it say, "To re-establish psychic balance for women war victims, by running their own households with support of Medica team, and by gaining better qualification through education"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And does it say, "To do sociological and analytical research"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And, Dr. Younggren, in the end, when they're explaining their goals, does it say that "staff as well as patients belong to all three ethnic groups of former Yugoslavia." And that's on that same page right afterwards, and that "We want to stick to this principle and maintain our independence although is growing, even in Zenica's nationalistic pressure"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a quote.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm just worried about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, I'd like to ask a couple questions about memory. You mentioned in your testimony yesterday that you believe that rape had an effect on memory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there's empirical evidence for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, and you cited the Koss study, sir; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, in the Koss study, which I have here, under the section of "Memories," it says: "Relatively modest magnitude for affecting those memories has been caused by rape." Are you familiar with that part of the study?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a copy of the study with me, and I'd like to have that, if I could?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask if we could have copies of where she's citing from so that the witness can also see the context.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that study, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do you have it with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: He needs to go get it. It's not with him, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's in my briefcase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the witness will be allowed to get his copy so he can refer to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I offer the witness a copy of my study?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Then the witness can come back and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, you see there I have two places highlighted in the study, and this is under the section of "Memories"; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: What those portions are saying, sir, isn't it, that the effect on memory is of a relatively modest magnitude after the occurrence of rape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That -- that quote is correct in the context of the rest of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. And, sir, the second part that's highlighted, doesn't it say "the effects were inconsistent in direction and magnitude"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and it also follows with the statement: "There were large and positive effects" -- let me see. "They were positive and large on the affect factor and negative and somewhat smaller on both clarity and sensitive."

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, doesn't that really mean that some things were remembered better and maybe some things were remembered less?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that that's what you mean by the effect on memory when you testified yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That rape affects memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you understand that that study was done with a population of university women who had been raped; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. It's a large survey, and they separated out those that were raped from individuals who had memories of bad experiences.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. And as a matter of fact, the population that they studied was a population of university women who were raped who were trying not to think about the rape; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've testified a bit about Post Traumatic Stress Syndrome, and one of the symptoms of Post Traumatic Stress Syndrome is intrusive memories; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is intrusive memory and avoidance of the stimuli, so that's one symptom, and you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, in terms of intrusive memories, that means that memories come back. You try to repress them but you can't repress them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They're experienced in different ways but, right, they pop through, if you will, the natural defence to try to avoid thinking about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And, sir, would you agree that this is a study that looked at memory as affected by rape, not memory as affected by Post Traumatic Stress Syndrome; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will say the study doesn't address that. It wasn't evaluating PTSD as such, it's a study about rape.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right. Are all people who are raped also sufferers of Post Traumatic Stress Syndrome?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all. There are many people that recover. I mean, there are a variety of things that occur. Not everyone develops PTSD.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And, sir, also in this study, the population of university women, to our knowledge, there was a single incidence of rape, wasn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so. I'd have to go back through the study.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And, sir, this study certainly did not take in war conditions or imprisonment conditions or serial or multiple rapes, did it, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's a study of the effects of rape upon memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, I just have a couple more questions that I would like to ask you, and one relates to your summarised expert witness statement. Are you -- I do have copies of this. I would like to ask the witness -- and for the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be marked as Prosecution Exhibit number 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, I'd like to direct you to your summarised witness statement, first paragraph, please. In the last sentence of the first paragraph, you state: "This is true of memories of intense and passive experiences, although intense experiences are logically remembered more accurately because of our tendency to attend to them more --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please? Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I understand that in the preceding sentence, to place this in context, haven't you stated that memory is reconstructive, and it easily follows that the longer the passage of time, the more inaccurate memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I believe the literature says.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, that's what you've written in your summarised statement; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Then, sir, in the next sentence, you do say that, "although intense experiences are logically remembered more accurately because of our tendency to attend to them more actively"; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, are you familiar with the concept of gist and peripheral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Would you agree that certain intense experiences become the gist experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, do you know how tall I am?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: In centimetres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Is that very important to me cross-examining you, how tall I am?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, I want to turn to your testimony yesterday and the testimony -- you stated that Witness A had a recollection of the Defendant as blond and short; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, what do you base that information upon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 1995 testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: You probably had a lot of information to absorb, a lot of documents to read, a lot of details to concentrate on before coming to give your testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, I would like to give you a copy of one page of the 1995 statement. I have copies for the rest of the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked Prosecution Exhibit number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, I would like to turn your attention to the next-to-the-last paragraph, and that would be the last three sentences on that next-to-last paragraph. Dr. Younggren, doesn't that say: "Anto was tall"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it says that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, you did not read in the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have the answer to that. What is 172 centimetres, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Beg your pardon, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know? What is 172 centimetres in feet and inches?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, might I ask -- Dr. Younggren, you are an American, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So am I. Do you usually deal in centimetres when you're talking about height?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: 172 centimetres is about five foot seven.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I actually asked for the conversion to understand the height, so I know it's five seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Do you know in centimetres the difference between 172 and 183 in terms of finger distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately three, four inches.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, can you show me three or four inches just with your ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd say approximately this (indicating).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 172 centimetres, to me, is short for a man.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sir, you didn't read in this document or any documents that you received that he was short with blond hair, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not read the word "short" in the document, I read 172 centimetres. That is approximately five foot seven inches tall, which is short for a man. The "short" appraisal is my appraisal. The document says tall, 172 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's what I was about to say: For which nation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beg your pardon, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: For which nation? If you say that's short; for which nation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, I would like to ask a couple other questions about the documents that you've read. You said that you are familiar with the transcripts of the case that took place in June; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, what is the effect of corroboration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Corroboration tends to confirm evidence, confirm memory. I mean, corroboration is a valuable part of establishing reality in -- I guess, properly, both a forensic and a clinical sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Younggren. Your Honour, might I just have a minute, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Younggren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Re-examination by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Younggren, Ms. Sellers asked you about Medica and about the fact that they were operating in a wartime situation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, what is your opinion as to whether treatment in a wartime situation, as opposed to a peacetime situation, is more difficult? Is it more difficult?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure it's more difficult. Of course it's more difficult. The stress level is substantially higher, plus, frankly, treatment goals in wartime are often very different from treatment goals in peacetime, from triage on down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Would it be an unusual or an exceptional situation then, based on what you just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that it is an exceptional situation, would that require someone with even more experience and understanding of treatment of trauma than the average psychologist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly you would assume that. It's a very complex situation, and I think that it would require a careful tuning of the techniques to address the prevalent stress that's going on under artillery fire while you're doing therapy. That's a little distracting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And given the fact that that would require -- may require someone with even more experience, what type of damage could be done to a person who is treated by people with no knowledge in the area of trauma while dealing in an exceptional situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, you can damage patients if you don't know how to deal with them. This is a serious disorder of long-term consequence. We have VA hospitals filled with veterans who have been exposed to combat, and I truly believe that the individuals who tried to help them did the best they could. I'm not so sure they did the right thing, and obviously, retrospectively, we know better now how to treat this disorder than we did the in the mid '40s, but it's clear that treating it wrong can have disastrous effects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Ms. Sellers took you through Defence 25 and read, basically, out of the document the different types of services that were provided to (sic) Medica. When you testified yesterday, were you attacking Medica overall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I think that for a group of individuals who go in a combat zone with the best of intentions, to help a population of people under siege that are starving, is laudatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers refreshed your recollection about the testimony of Dr. Mujenznovic with respect to Dr. Sabic, and referred you to the fact that Dr. Mujenznovic recalls Dr. Sabic saying that you gradually have the patient discuss the traumatic event. Isn't that what happened on cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That’s exactly what happened

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It had to have been. That's the only way they would have this information, unless someone else told them about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know if California State hospitals also have a political purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it your experience that hospitals have, as part of their stated objectives, the accomplishment of any political or social objectives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, for many of the non-profit hospitals, that would create some significant problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in your experience working in hospitals, does any hospital you know ask a physician, a therapist, et cetera, to also partake in any kind of political objective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now -- so would it be unusual, in your experience, to have a treatment centre have as one of its stated objectives the prosecution of war criminals?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I don't believe that that's contained within any of the Medica documents, unless learned counsel would like to refer us to where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I refer to D25, page 5 that we discussed yesterday. Second to last page, Doctor. Under the area of "Research." One of their objectives is, "While our mobile teams visits the refugee camps, they also collect data on refugees in order to understand and analyse the full dimension of war violence against women in ex-Yugoslavia." And in the next line is, "Summon international law courts against war criminals."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any experience with any institutions that have a similar objective with respect to prosecuting, let's say, everyday criminals in California, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm going to give you the opportunity to explain the sentence that Ms. Sellers brought your attention to on cross-examination, and that sentence was, "This is true of memories of intense and passive experiences, although intense experiences are logically remembered more accurately because of our tendency to attend to them more actively." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, simply put, if you have an experience that is emotionally meaningful in the sense of intense, it tends to be registered better than passing -- passive experiences like passing a stop sign while you're driving, or, you know, people's dress in a shopping centre and so forth. Those are obviously memories. And I made that statement really addressing the conflict between gist and peripheral as well, that sometimes in the midst of very intense experiences, I will say horribly intense experiences, there are pieces of data that are more passive and are not stored properly, and I will call these peripheral details. So that the theme or the gist of intense experiences is remembered better, and I think that research clearly supports that. The peripheral details are prone to distortion, and we can get lost in a debate about what is or isn't peripheral, but I think that there is evidence in the materials, as well as in the testimony, for the loss of peripheral detail about what occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On that same page, down at the bottom, you made the statement, "This likely contaminated the accuracy of her recollections of her experiences due to the tendency of trauma victims to try to organise what they experienced into something that is meaningful." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, from a therapeutic perspective, meaningful is important. I won't say it's important to every victim, but for people to organise what happened to them into something that's sensible and meaningful is just simply helpful, because the confusion can be emotionally destructive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, is it your experience that trauma patients have any disjointed memory, or is it in the studies that trauma patients have scattered memories about the events in question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Frequently scattered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that a victim of trauma could have transposed one memory over the top of another one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's exactly what that says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me for interrupting. I'd like to ask could we go into closed session at this point in time? We're getting into details of the testimony that were not brought out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we went into explicit detail in closing argument where no one had an objection, where we were talking about what the issues in the case were. Those closing arguments are available on the Internet, and these are the exact same issues that have been discussed over and over again and are public. There's no reason, given the fact that names will not be revealed, that these issues shouldn't be made public.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might say, we've already had inadvertent admissions that have occurred today. There's information that we got yesterday that was not part of the public documents. I would just ask, for the protection of the witness, which this Court has granted complete and thorough protection, that we try and be consistent and, I think, to go into closed session as we go into these details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think we'll go into closed session, considering that the evidence of Witness A was heard in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Right, but --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Private session or closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Private session. We'll go into private session, without pulling down the blinds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Could you state your full name and spell your last name for the court reporter, please?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: My name is Charles Alexander Morgan, M-O-R-G-A-N, the III.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: You are a doctor, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And of what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: May I interrupt, Mr. Davidson? We have the CV of this witness, and I would like to ask the Prosecution whether they have an objection to having it admitted into evidence, the CV only.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: No objection at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In which case it doesn't require you to go into details of the CV. It is before the Court. You can proceed with the substance of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: We will mark the CV as the next Defence exhibit, which I believe is 26.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, D26.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I have made extra copies for the Judges if they want them. So with the stipulation regarding the CV, I will go directly into substance questions and not detail the witness's background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Morgan, how long have you been at Yale University?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I've been at Yale University for the past nine years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And that is located where?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: In New Haven, Connecticut in the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Since 1989 have you specialised in the area of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, I have. That's the area of my speciality and the focus of all my research.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: As -- I'll use the term PTSD rather than using Post Traumatic Stress Disorder on a constant basis; all right? Has PTSD been accepted as a diagnosable mental disorder?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And when was it so accepted?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, PTSD, was officially accepted and recognised by the psychiatric community in 1982, and was published in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual, the DSM III, and after that DSM IIIR and now DSM IV.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I take it the definition of PTSD has changed over the years till today?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: There have been some minor modifications in how we describe the traumatic event and the ordering of specific symptoms of PTSD, and also one modification that emphasises that a clinician must note significant impairment in an individual's life to make the diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Now, have you prepared any chart for us today relating to the details -- or the definition of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: What I would like to do, Your Honours, if I may, is to have the witness put on the ELMO a chart, strictly to help the parties follow the testimony as he gives the definition of PTSD. And I have extra copies here and I would like to mark them as Defence Exhibit 26 . Twenty seven?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I'm slightly un -- I'm unfamiliar with how to work this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Morgan can you tell the Trial Chamber what PTSD is and take us through each of the elements so we understand what PTSD is as a basis for my later questions in this case?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes. Post Traumatic Stress Disorder is a name that's given to a specific condition that can be diagnosed in people exposed to a traumatic event. So I've put on the chart as event number 1, exposure to a traumatic event. The event must be, according to the early definition, had to be a catastrophic or overwhelming event. The most recent definitions according to DSM 4 are more precise and so the person must believe that their physical integrity or life is directly threatened and that they may have intense feelings of horror, shock or helplessness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: You have to slow down a little bit?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Sorry. Examples of traumatic events are things like rape, war trauma, seeing people shot, blown up. It could be something like a tornado destroying someone's home, mud slides, events where people die and where a person fears that they themselves may be killed. It is not typically used to describe a condition where someone loses their pet, where their pet animal may die. It is not used as a definition for the loss of the -- what's considered to be the expected loss of a family member, someone dying of old age in the family. If someone's child should suddenly die and it's unexpected that would be categorised as a traumatic event, but there are certain events that are not included in this definition. The next item is symptom clusters, and I've done that -- and I've put three items below that, re-experiencing, avoidance and numbing, and hyperarousal. Those are the three broad terms that describe the symptoms that a person with PTSD may exhibit. The re-experiencing simply refers to things like having uncontrollable thoughts. So, for example if a woman has been raped, she may describe the symptoms of; "I can't stop thinking about things, it keeps coming back into my mind when I don't want it to." Having nightmares or bad dreams about the traumatic event. A combat veteran may say, "I keep dreaming of the shells exploding or seeing my buddy blown up." An extreme form of remembering a trauma is called "a flashback," and that refers to a condition where someone feels as if the trauma is happening all over again. They feel that they can see the event and possibly smell what was going on and hear what was going on. The avoidance and numbing items are typically described as, people may say, "I feel as though I can't go on living, I feel like I want to die, I can't feel close to other people," there's an estrangement from other people. They also describe symptoms of avoidance, trying to stay away from things that remind them of what's happened to them. So, for example, someone may say, "When I see my body where I was injured or I see a film about war, I get these thoughts in my head that are very uncomfortable and I try to put them out of my mind right away. I try and stay busy, I try and stay focused because I don't want to think about what's happened to me because it's very upsetting." Those types of symptoms go under "avoidance" and "numbing." To clinicians who may not be familiar with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, these symptoms can look very much like the symptoms of depression. The hyperarousal cluster is a group of symptoms where people describe things like "Everything irritates me, I'm jumpy when I hear loud sounds," feeling angry, having sleeping trouble, difficulty falling asleep, difficulty concentrating. The duration criterion is to help clinicians pay attention to how long a person has had these symptoms. So they make sure a person has experienced a traumatic event, they look at the symptoms that they're describing, and then they find out how long they've had them. If a person has had these symptoms for at least a month, for four weeks, then they can receive a diagnosis of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, not before. If they have the symptoms after three months, at least three months and longer, then we make it a little more clear when we refer to Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and we say it's Post Traumatic Stress Disorder of a chronic type, meaning that it's lasted longer. The distinction is important because chronic Post Traumatic Stress Disorder reflects a more severe form of the disorder. The clinical impairment item I put on there because it's also one of the newer emphases in DSM IV reminding clinicians to make an assessment as to whether or not the traumatic event, the experience of being traumatised, has changed someone's life; for example, are they no longer able to work as they used to? Are they no longer able to feel close to other people in the way that they used to? Do they not keep up their person, their grooming, their everyday life? Do they view the world differently? It's to get a sense of how hard the experience has been on their life.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: So when a person meets all of these standards and it lasts for longer than three months, it is diagnosed as chronic PTSD?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Is there any known cure for chronic PTSD?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: To the best of our knowledge, no, there is not a known cure for chronic Post Traumatic Stress Disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Have there been any studies reflecting the length of time that a person will suffer from chronic PTSD?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: There have been a large number of studies on that, and they have mainly been studies looking at combat veterans from World War II, from the Vietnam war, but more recently there are studies that have included more women, women who have suffered from sexual assault and rape and who have Post Traumatic Stress Disorder as a result of that. Taken together, those studies suggest that people may have chronic PTSD for at least up to 30 to 40 and now, in World War II veterans, maybe 50 years after they've been traumatised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Is there a series of waxing and waning of the symptoms?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: You mean does it sort of get worse and sometimes better? Oh, yes. A number of studies now show that at any given time over the years, a person may appear more sick than at other times. In general, the -- sometimes, in some people, those periods of looking worse happen spontaneously. There doesn't seem to be a reason why they suddenly feel worse. What we do know for sure is that people will get worse when we put them around reminders of the event. So for veterans, it may be Veterans' Day or Armistice Day, maybe seeing a movie or a parade. You can see an increase in the symptoms if someone maybe has a death in the family or a crisis, something stressful kicks up the body's stress response and they feel worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Even when that event is unassociated with the original trauma?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Such as the death of a mother might bring back symptoms relating to an earlier trauma?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes. We now know that to be true, that a person's PTSD symptoms can increase when they are confronted with a stress that is unrelated to their previous trauma.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Morgan, in preparing for testimony here today, did you review the documents which have been admitted into evidence relating to Witness A's interviews and diagnosis at Medica?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: So you've reviewed the Medica documents?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: What do those documents reflect, if anything, with respect to Medica's diagnosis of Witness A's psychological condition?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: My reading of the documents suggest that the people who evaluated her concluded that she was suffering from Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and that they were -- it appears they were relying on DSM IV criteria. My reading of the document also suggests to me that someone did history-taking, they took a history in some way. There's a very detailed description at the beginning of the document about what Witness A experienced as her traumatic event where it mentions the names of two individuals who sexually abused her, raped her; and following that description, there is a mentioning of specific symptoms, such as, as I mentioned under re-experiencing, there are segments of the document that refer to "uncontrolled thoughts" about the event; there are symptoms of avoidance where there's reference to Witness A trying not to think about the events; there are symptoms of sleep

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak a little more slowly, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If the witness -- can you speak more slowly? The interpreters have to follow.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The clinical impairment items are also suggested to me in that document where someone's come for treatment and they believe she's in need of treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the translation to catch up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Morgan, have there been any studies with respect to the biological and psychological factors of persons suffering from chronic PTSD?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, there have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Have the majority of those studies been with people with chronic PTSD vis-à-vis acute PTSD, that is, that PTSD which hasn't lasted three months?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The majority of studies have been in chronic PTSD because people started studying combat veterans, and by the very definition, they'd been out of the war for more than three months, so they had chronic Post Traumatic Stress Disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what the studies have revealed with respect to the psychological factors associated with persons with chronic PTSD?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Taken together, the studies that have been conducted in World War II veterans, Vietnam combat veterans, rape victims, adults with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder from child abuse that they've never forgotten about have all shown -- and this is now reflected in DSM -- that the psychological symptoms of PTSD are the same regardless of how people got Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. You get the same disorder whether or not you were in a horrible car accident or if you were in a horrible spot in a war zone or if you were raped and held in captivity, the symptoms are the same, and that's why, under the DSM, there is no provisional statement that says PTSD due to car accident, PTSD due to rape, PTSD due to trauma X. Our profession and our colleagues recognise that the illness is the same. The other thing that we have learned from studies for the psychological aspects of chronic Post Traumatic Stress Disorder is that people who have developed chronic PTSD are usually the people who early on, while the trauma was happening or shortly thereafter, had the greatest number of symptoms of PTSD and who had high levels of shock, disorientation, and confusion. Technically, in our field, we refer to those symptoms as "dissociation" or "dissociative symptoms," and there are examples of that in Witness A's statement where she refers to losing track of the time, where things happen in a moment or a moment takes forever or she sat frozen and still, not feeling anything, no fear, no nothing, not feeling her body, and if you want the precise words, I'll have to get the document and read it, but those are examples of dissociative symptoms; and we know that people who have higher levels of those kind of symptoms early on in a traumatic event are most likely to be the people who have gone on to develop chronic Post Traumatic Stress Disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber about those studies which deal with the biological factors of persons suffering from chronic PTSD?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes. I will summarise the findings of the enormous number of studies because there's an enormous amount of research now. In our institution, at the National Center for PTSD, that's one of our main goals and we do an enormous amount of research on this. Taken together, we know a couple of things for sure. It's not speculative, it's firmly accepted in the scientific community. We know for sure that in people with PTSD, there are abnormalities in their bodies' stress response, in the amount of stress hormones they produce under stress, and in their bodies' reaction to those stress hormones. We know specifically that people with PTSD have abnormal functioning in the adrenaline systems of the body and we know specifically that they have an abnormality in their bodies' stress hormone response to glucocorticoids. I'll spell that. G-L-U-C-O-R-T-I-C-O-I-D-S (sic). Glucocorticoids and adrenaline are necessary for our body to respond to stress. When we're under stress and we're frightened, our body produces a -- those chemicals. We know in a normal setting, those chemicals are helpful. They help us pay attention, they orient us to danger, and they help us remember what's going on. However, we also know that under extraordinary circumstances, where there's a life-threatening event, the levels of these hormones are very high, and we know that they can cause damage and actually destroy areas -- brain cells and damage areas of the brain. We know that from animal studies, we know that now in studies in humans. Specifically we know that high levels of adrenaline disrupt attention, and without proper attention, your brain does not properly record information. We know that high levels of glucocorticoids damage the specific areas of the brain that are responsible for making memories for fearful things and -- I'll stop there. What's the damage? What do we know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we stop there? It's time for our break. It is 11.05, we shall have a break for 30 minutes and resume at 11.35.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Doctor, I think we left off, just before the break, with respect to your testimony relating to possible brain damage.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Can you pick it up from there, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes. What I had mentioned was that an area of the brain called the hippocampus, that's responsible for how we learn specific things in memory, is damaged by high levels of stress hormones. What that area of the brain does is it let's us know the timing, and the context and characteristics of an event. It sort of puts it in a setting. And we know that in ample studies, if that area is damaged, the animal, if it's learned where something bad happened to it or how to travel through a maze, can't do it properly. We know in humans -- we don't damage people's brains to do research -- but there's a very elegant study done by a man named Kirschbaum who gave healthy subjects high levels of glucocorticoids and wanted to see what happened to their memory. So he had them learn several different kinds of memory tests, not only what they could recall about what they'd learned on a test, but could they actually remember where things were in a room, how many objects, and actually redraw it and correctly give that information back? His study has shown that when you increase -- the people who got the glucocorticoids in high doses were significantly less able, in other words, they did much more poorly on these specific tests, on their memory performance on the tests, and that's one of the most direct ways we can measure the effects of glucocorticoids in healthy subjects. Now, in PTSD -- in people with PTSD, since they've already been traumatised, the studies have sort of been worked a little bit in the opposite direction, because we're starting with someone who's already been through a trauma, and, we assume, already had those high levels of stress hormones. There are a number of several studies now in people with PTSD from rape, in combat veterans with did PTSD, that just in giving them neurologic testing on recall memory, asking them to learn words, learn information and then recall it back, on their free recall they actually score more poorly than people without Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. And that points to a specific problem in that area of the brain. We know that's the area that's responsible. A second line of research that doesn't ask people directly what they know is my specific area of research, is in the human startle reflex. It is a direct way of measuring what that area of the brain is recording. It's a direct reflex that is the same in humans and in animals. What we have found is that people with PTSD cannot distinguish between a dangerous stimulus in the room and a non-dangerous stimulus in the room, and I'd like to explain that. It was -- it's a study. What I do is called fear conditioning. I teach people to learn that a light in the room will be associated with an electric shock on the wrist, and it's very unpleasant. People learn very quickly that the purple light is bad, that when the purple light comes into the room they get an electric shock. Healthy people quickly learn that when the yellow light comes into the room that there is no shock, and that there is no possibility that they will get a shock. We do these studies to look at how quickly or well people learn something, and then we re-test them a week later to see what they remember. The startle reflex is a direct way of measuring what they know. You don't have to ask them, you bring-- you just turn on the purple light and the startle reflex will only increase in the presence of the light that was paired with shock, and it will only increase when they're tested in the context where they received the shock if they get back in that same chair where they were sitting when got they got the shock on the wrist. We've done this in animal studies. Animals get foot shocks. People, we give them a shock on the wrist. What we find in people with PTSD when we compared them to people without PTSD, we found that they were unable to tell the difference between which light gave them -- was associated with shock. They were also unable to predict the timing. So this was another area of research that let us know that the area of the brain in animals and in people that is responsible for people being able to tell the difference is the hippocampus. So that was another piece of evidence saying -- here is another body of research saying there's damage in this area of the brain. Finally, several of my colleagues at Yale do brain imaging studies, and there are a number of other investigators over the States who have done brain imaging studies where they actually do pictures of the brain to measure what these areas of the brain look like. There are at least four published studies, and I know a fifth that is in the process of being published, it's now being presented at an international conference, that the hippocampus is significantly damaged, it's smaller, it's shrunk in people with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. So putting aside any other issue of people talking to patients or whatnot, just from a statement of biology, research in the field of PTSD says that the area of the brain that helps us learn these things and sort this kind of information out has been damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Now, in 1997 and 1998, were there any controlled studies relating to persons with PTSD, whether the PTSD was acute or chronic, vis-à-vis the recitations of these persons with reported memory?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, there have been a number of studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: But prior to 1997, were there any studies relating to the stability of traumatic memories using as subjects persons with PTSD?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: To my knowledge there are no studies that specifically used persons with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Prior to 1997, were there any studies relating to the stability of traumatic memories with persons who had heard or had knowledge about traumatic events but which persons did not have PTSD?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And can you describe to the Trial Chamber the nature of those studies?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Prior to 1997, several studies had been done that were trying to answer the question of do people remember terrible things better than neutral things, better than everyday events. A very famous study in 1970's and early '80's was by Brown and Kulik, Brown and his colleagues, Dr. Brown and Kulik, who interviewed people and asked them what they remembered when the United States President John F. Kennedy was assassinated. They asked people, "Do you remember where you were, do you remember what you were doing, do you remember what you were feeling?" They were struck by the fact that the subjects they interviewed provide a lot of detail about where they were, what they were doing, and seemed to be very sure of their recollections for how they heard about the assassination and what they thought. And they took the clarity of those recollections and the conviction on the part of the subjects as evidence that people remember bad things better than neutral things, and they coined the term "Flashbulb memories". They felt that going through or hearing about a terrible thing just imprinted the memory in a person's mind like a photographic plate. That's why they referred to this as flashbulb. After their study, another group, Winograd and her group, did a replication of the study. They too asked people about what they recalled, about where they were, how they got the information when President Kennedy was assassinated. I believe in their study they also asked about some other events. I believe the assassination of Martin Luther King was also in that study. I'm not sure. I'd have to check for that. They too found that people were very sure where they were, what they were thinking and what they were feeling. Those researchers concluded that people were very sure, and that they provided detail, and they made a point in their paper saying, "We have no idea if this is accurate at all, but we are impressed that people provide detail." After those studies, people got interested in pursuing this idea that memories for trauma were flashbulb in nature, or photographic in nature. And there is a series of studies that asked people where they were and how they heard about the explosion of the space shuttle Challenger. There is a series of studies. Some of the studies interviewed college students shortly after the explosion, and then re-interviewed them approximately a year later. Another study caught up with people a couple of years later. What they found was that people were highly inconsistent, that the second time they were interviewed they changed where they were. So, for example, some students said, "I know exactly where I was. I was in class. I heard the news. I was with friend so and so, and I'm sure of it." When they re-interviewed them, they found that people said, "No. I heard about it when I was home and I wasn't with anybody." So people began to question this flashbulb nature of memory, and they said, well, they've got some element right. They knew the space shuttle blew up, but they were struck by the fact that people's stories had changed. A similar study was done around looking at how citizens in Sweden remembered the assassination of Olof Palme.
