They were interviewed, I think, approximately six weeks after the assassination, and I believe close to a year later but sometime later, and the author in that study had two conclusions. His main conclusion was that people remembered that there had been an assassination, but depending on how you defined a flashbulb memory, it was either a little over 50 per cent accuracy or 90 per cent accurate. If you defined flashbulb memory as just saying you remembered the source of your information and what happened, people were pretty good. Ninety per cent, still 10 per cent didn't get that right. But if you pushed for detail, it dropped to 50 per cent. Now, these were people who, as far as we know, do not have Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and were not patients. So the criticism of those studies was that these studies don't tell us anything about traumatic memories, because those people were not personally threatened. They heard about horrible things on the news, but their lives were not in danger. And so those studies, they're fine, they're nice. They tell us that, yeah, people remember bad things better than neutral things, but it doesn't tell us anything about trauma and memory. So we decided to conduct a study in people whose lives had been personally threatened in a war zone, and I've prepared a chart --

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, in 1997 and 1998, how many studies were there relating to persons with PTSD, both chronic and acute, vis-à-vis their recitations of reported memory?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: There have been four studies in 1997, 1998. Three of those studies are published. The fourth study is currently in review and being evaluated for publication, and has been presented at two international conferences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Let me ask a few questions concerning the studies before we go directly to the studies?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Were all four of the studies about which you're going to testify controlled studies?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what you mean by a controlled study?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: A controlled study is a study where a person has been interviewed, or asked questions or assessed more than once. In other words, it's a test-retest study. And at both time points, in order to make it a scientific study, a controlled study will use the same assessment procedure. You'll use the same measure so that you can answer the question of, "Do people tell me the same thing if I ask them exactly the same questions at two different time points?" The distinction is important, because a number of people have conducted studies, but they have not been controlled. In other words, they might have researched in the past to find some information about someone and then used that as support to say their memory's accurate, but, in fact, different people did the earlier questions, may not have asked the questions in the same way, and as a result, scientifically, our conclusions on those studies must be limited. So in a controlled study, we want to make sure we use the same criteria, the same rules each time we assess the person's memory or whatever we're assessing. The studies in 1997 and 1998 have used that methodology. In each of the studies, people in those studies were interviewed or assessed shortly after experiencing life-threatening personal events. Either seeing people shot beside them, being shot at, being injured in a war zone, or people who had survived a mass shooting in Texas in the United States. At each of those time points, the people in the studies were reassessed using the same methods that they had been assessed -- that had been used on them in their first interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Doctor, how did the subjects in the tests in 1997 and 1998 differ from those persons who were used in the tests prior to 1997?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Subjects in these studies were different in that, one, their lives were personally threatened, there was a real risk they could die, and that people did die around them in the events they experienced, and they too believed that they might die. That's very different than in the other studies. They were people who have never forgotten in terms of saying, "I was there," in terms of saying, "Yes, I was at the shoot-out at Texas," "Yes, I was in Desert Storm." So this is very different from the field of recovered memory, where in that field that is a separate area of investigation from studies in Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. And I would like to say this, because I think sometimes people confuse the fields; in the recovered memory field, we're talking about people who at some point in time meet with a therapist and have symptoms, and then they go looking for a trauma to explain the symptoms. In our work at the National Centre for Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and in the DSM IV guidelines, you must start with a traumatic event and then examine symptoms relating to that traumatic event. So our studies and the studies I'm going to talk about are about people who were in these events as adults, who were exposed to life-threatening events as adults, and who have been assessed while they're adults using the same methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: The person -- are all the persons in the tests people with PTSD?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Explain why people without PTSD are included in the test group.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Well, first it's the way of things. Not everyone gets Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. It is a widely held misconception that everyone gets PTSD. In fact, there are at least three large epidemiological studies in the United States, from inner cities, that show that the rates of PTSD are approximately nine per cent. So many people have a misconception that everyone exposed to trauma gets PTSD. It is absolutely not true. When you look in a particular group of people, people who have suffered rape or people who have been tortured, although that represents a minority of cases of PTSD, it's more likely that a person will get PTSD from rape than from a car accident. The risk of getting it is much more great, and people believe that because the person's life was more directly threatened in some way by another human being. However, three different studies have been conducted and have documented that of all the women who experience rape, when they are assessed three months after their rape, less than half have PTSD. The highest figure I have been able to find is 47 per cent. Clearly that's a lot of people, but it is less than half.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Let's turn to -- what was the first test of the kind that you've described conducted in 1997?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: All right. I've prepared a chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: First, tell me what the test was.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Oh, the test was we -- we interviewed men and women from an army unit who had been in the Gulf War, from the United States, and whose unit had in some way experienced trauma and they came back with fewer unit members. We knew for sure that people had died in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Who was the author of that study?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: The first author of that study is my boss Professor Stephen Southwick from Yale University, and it was with him -- he and I conducted the study.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I would like to have the witness use this on the ELMO. I have extra copies for the Court, I have copies for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D28.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters would like to ask the witness to speak slowly, please. [Note: Interpreter's comments obliterates Mr. Davidson's question]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Witness, the interpreter would like you to speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry. The slide I've prepared mentions the first author, Dr. Southwick. Under the word "Subjects," that indicates that we had interviewed men and women who were in the army unit and that these individuals, we met with them and gave them a particular set of questionnaires one month after they came back from the Gulf War and during the same month two years later. On the next slide, I put a brief comment that our questionnaires were designed to ask them specific things that they may or may not have experienced in the Gulf, and those specific things were questions like: Was your unit ambushed? Was it overrun? Did you see someone killed? Did you witness the death of a friend? Did you see the bizarre disfigurement of other humans? Questions like that. And the subjects in the study could indicate "Yes" or "No," they did or didn't experience those things, and they could also indicate how many times, so we would be able to look at whether -- how many times they had had an event happen. On the next page, the total score. This was a way of summing up the points on the questionnaires, and that was made by adding up every time they said "Yes, this happened to me." What we found is that from one month to two years, their score increased, and this indicated that their answers had changed significantly. When we looked at it, we found that 88 per cent of our subjects changed at least one item, 61 per cent changed two or more. Now, that didn't sound like very many things to change on a questionnaire until we started looking at the items, and we found that people changed every kind of item on the questionnaire. So, for example, down below, it says "No" to "Yes" around 70 per cent of our subjects categorically went from saying "No, I did not experience this" to "Yes, I did --" I'm too fast. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: And 46 per cent, nearly half of our subjects, a bit less than half, said, "No, I did not experience this" when we asked them at the two-year time point. On the last page, I've listed the five items that were the most commonly changed, and as you will notice, some of them seem a little more subjective than others, whether or not a person felt that there was an extreme threat to their personal safety, whereas others seemed more objective, did they or did they not see someone killed or see somebody wounded or experience a mine or a booby trap. We also found that people with PTSD changed their answers much more and that they were more likely, when we interviewed them at the two-year time point, to say they had seen more trauma. This surprised us because we had not expected that people's reports of traumatic memories would change. In our field, we had been working on the assumption that, if you go through something terrible, you don't forget it. So these results caught our attention right away because they do not support the idea that memory or reported memory for a traumatic event stays the same. The next study that was done was not by our group, it was done by a Dr. Roemer, and I've prepared a slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I have extra copies --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: -- and we'll hand them to the registrar, a copy for each member of the Court, and he has an extra one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D29.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I am missing my slide of Dr. Roemer. It's all right --

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: We have one. I want it on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Dr. Roemer --

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us who Dr. Roemer is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Roemer is a scientist who conducts research in Post Traumatic Stress Disorder up at Boston University.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us the nature of her study and the results therefrom?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes. The nature of her study was very similar to our first study. She assessed the reports of what people saw and experienced at two time points. Specifically, she asked questions of 460 men and women who had been deployed to Somalia from the United States. She too found that 33 per cent of the subjects were significantly inconsistent, they reported something different when they filled out the same questionnaires 21 months later. She also found that the more symptoms of PTSD and the people that had PTSD changed their answers the most. So this study confirmed our findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Doctor, let me ask you, in the studies that you have just gone through and those which you are going to go through, they deal with inconsistencies; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Is there a difference here in the terminology between inconsistencies and accuracies in terms of what these tests are measuring?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I believe there is, and I should say something about that. In interviewing people and asking them what they saw and what they did, we don't know of any way of actually determining exactly what happened in a war zone. We did know from the news that in the units that we studied that people were killed -- and we knew that because they were from Connecticut and their bodies were returned to Connecticut -- however, we had no independent objective source of information against which we could compare their reports. So we believe that we would simply document whether or not there were changes in what people said without knowing how accurate any of their responses were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Now, consistencies or inconsistencies provide an indirect way of looking at accuracy in this sense: Some of the responses are mutually exclusive where someone says "I was shot," "No, I was not shot." We felt that the two would be mutually exclusive, so it was possible that that would be an inaccurate statement. However, we also know that even if a person says the same thing both times, if they're consistent, that they could be wrong both times. So that looking at inconsistencies only provides us an indirect way at times of examining accuracy in the absence of some external source of information. I think Dr. Roemer and her group experienced the same problem: They found they could not get an independent report from the United States government on exactly what happened and they too concluded that inconsistency was the best anyone could do since we can't know exactly what people know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: The next report was done by Professor North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Let me mark that -- do you have a copy there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: No, those are the two I'm missing, actually. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D30.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Dr. Carol North conducted a study, a controlled study, and she interviewed people who had experienced the shoot-out in Texas. Someone had come into a store or a restaurant and began shooting people. She interviewed the survivors approximately a month after they had witnessed the event, and she re-interviewed the survivors one year later. What is striking about her study is that 21 per cent of her subjects and nearly half of the subjects with PTSD, when interviewed one year later, denied ever having nightmares, ever having uncontrollable thoughts about the shooting, ever having irritability, they denied ever trying not to think about it; in other words, they denied ever having been ill. At one month, those were people who had clearly said to the interviewer, because they were doing direct interviews to make the diagnoses, they would have had to say things like "Yes, I have nightmares," "Yes, I can't stop thinking about this," "Yes, I have startle," "Yes, I have irritability," or "Yes, everything irritates me"; and when re-interviewed a year later said, "No, I never had uncontrollable thoughts," "No, I don't know what you're talking about. I've never been sick." "No, I don't really have sleeping trouble" or "No, I'm not irritated by everyone or any thing." And I have to tell you, as I sat in this courtroom yesterday and listened to Witness A, all I could think about was this study, because my understanding, after reading her statements, reading the statements from Medica, and listening to the doctor who testified yesterday morning, was that here is someone who was diagnosed with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder and who listed symptoms and who, in the courtroom yesterday, said, "No, I never had this. I never had uncontrollable thoughts, I never had irritability. I never felt this way." To me, that's completely compatible with this study. This is what Dr. North also found, and she found that in her subjects who had Post Traumatic Stress Disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Now, the fourth study was conducted when, and who participated in that study?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: The fourth study was conducted by me and by Dr. Steven Southwick, and we conducted this study because I wanted to double-check our findings. I told you earlier we did this study and interviewed people one month and two years after they got back from the war, and I didn't know why people had changed their answers and I wanted to try and find out why. We recontacted our subjects --

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Let me mark this.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: It would be D31.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, D31.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Do you have a copy there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO, please. Can you tell us the nature of the study and the results that were reached?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: The nature of the study is it's a controlled study, we're using the same assessment procedure, and it's conducted by the same researchers in the same subjects. We used an additional questionnaire. The first time, when I told you about our results, I mentioned the Desert Storm Trauma Questionnaire, DSTQ. The CES are the initials for the Combat Exposure Scale, and it is considered the standard in the field of psychiatry for assessing exposure to trauma and we've used it as the standard in research for Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. One of the criticisms of our first study was that we had used a scale that people didn't know very well so they didn't know how to understand our data. This time, we included the Combat Exposure Scale after people had completed the Desert Storm questionnaire. Finally, after people had completed the questionnaires, I interviewed them. I surprised them and said, "I'd like to spend some time now and talk to you." And I showed them their questionnaires from one month and from two years and asked them to help me understand the changes on the questionnaires. Once they had given me their explanation, I then showed them their six-year questionnaire and asked them to help me understand the significant changes that happened across all three time points. On the next slide, I believe it's this slide here --

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Just to summarise about -- compared these findings to the earlier findings. Once again, we found significant numbers of people changed categorically from two years to six years. Forty-one per cent of the subjects in the study went from saying "No" to "Yes" and from "Yes" to "No." Seventy-two per cent of the subjects did either. So we're not talking about a tiny fraction of people in the study. People were changing answers all over. They did it on both questionnaires, and you can see by the percentages, they're not very different from one another. Changes are going on. People are going from saying "Yes, this happened to me," "No, this did not." We had an example multiple times of people saying, "Yes, I saw five people killed." At the two-year time point they'd say, "No, I didn't see anyone killed," and at six years they'd say, "Yes, I saw one person killed." Another person said to me, "I saw no one killed. I did not see a friend killed." At the two-year time point, he had put, "Yes, I saw two friends killed." At the six-year time point, he said, "I saw one person killed." I remember asking him, and he said to me, he said, "Well, maybe the first time they weren't my friends, and so I said 'No, no one was killed.' But maybe by two years later, I thought, we were all in the war zone, people died, they were probably my friends 'cause we're all in the army, so I said two people." He had no explanation as to why he changed his answer at the last time point. Another person who had gone from saying "No, I didn't see anybody killed" -- or, excuse me, from "Yes, I did" to "No, I did not" back to -- and then stated "No" explained that he had been shown a photograph, and he assumed that he must have somehow confused the photograph in his mind with what he actually did or did not experience. Other subjects told me that listening to the news, listening to the radio, talking to friends may have altered their reports. Now, as someone who has been focused in neurobiology of PTSD, my first thought is we know that stress can damage the brain and these are the sorts of changes that you might predict based on knowing what that area of the brain does, it alters the context and the timing, but the subjects didn't appeal to brain pathology, they said, no, they appealed to other social things like the radio, the news, the television, or talking to people. Some even said, "I just must have forgot." And you'd say, "Well then, later on, you endorsed it," and they had no explanation. They were very frustrated in trying to come up with explanations for the discrepancies on these papers. The one thing that was absolutely clear is that all but one subject was certain that the six-year report was the most accurate. They said that was the most accurate account of what happened to them. One person differed and she said, "No, the two-year and the six-year report are the most accurate," and they differed from one another, and I asked her how that could be true and she said that the two-year was the most emotionally accurate but the six-year was the most factually accurate. I do not know if any of it is accurate because they clearly are inconsistent with one another. What we did find when we had people who were not in the study come and look at our data, soldiers who were in the Gulf who did not partake of our study, just to look at the data, and we asked them, we said, "What do you think? How would you explain this?" They were convinced that the first report would be the most accurate, and they also assured me that if they had done the study, they would never have changed an answer. So we were struck by that as researchers, feeling that people are always absolutely sure of what they would do or they can be very sure of what they said they went through, but apart from any independent evidence, we were completely convinced that people are significantly wrong or inaccurate or inconsistent. The precise term I should say would be they are significantly inconsistent because we do not know what's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Doctor, let's turn now -- we have about 15 minutes here before the 12.30 break -- and let's turn now to Witness A's treatment at Medica. That's one of the issues that we are here at this hearing to discuss. You have had an opportunity, and I think you have been provided there at the witness table, documents which are marked 22, 24, and 25 that relate to Medica and, specifically, I think it's 22 that deals with her interviews at Medica. Maybe that's 24.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I believe it's 24 -- 24 on mine is marked from Medica, the report from Medica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Before I ask you a question, just a thought occurred to me, that in the studies that -- in all four of the studies that you've discussed here today, you had people with both PTSD and people without PTSD. In all four of those studies, was there any consistency with respect to whether the people -- there were more inconsistencies with one group rather than another?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes. I did neglect to say this. In our first study, in Dr. Roemer's study, and in our second study, we have found that people with PTSD have significantly more inconsistencies than people without PTSD. We also found that it is along a spectrum: The more symptoms somebody has, we now find the more inconsistent they are, but the PTSD patients were at the high end of who changed their answers the most. So all three studies now, the two published, and this one's currently in review, but the data support this idea that PTSD and memory are complicated but that what people say they remember may really be a symptom of how bad they're feeling rather than being something independent, and for a long time in our field we've assumed that the report of trauma is independent of how sick you are: either you had it or you didn't. And now we're finding that the report of what people say they experienced is just the other -- it's another way of saying "How sick do you feel?" "How distressed do you feel?" In our latest study -- and I have to say it has not been published, so you may want to consider this in a slightly different weight -- we actually found that people with PTSD changed their answers in both directions: That the sicker they were, the more they changed their answers. But it went up or down. It wasn't necessarily true that they always said, "Oh, I saw more trauma." But all three studies are consistent in that they show that the sicker you are, the more your answers change.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Let's go back to the Medica reports. Based upon your review of the reports regarding Medica, do you have an opinion, Doctor, as to the type of therapy Witness A was receiving, according to those reports, at Medica?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber, please, what your opinion is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: The document is limited in what can be determined from it, but my reading of this tells me that whatever therapy was done, someone met with Witness A and tried to establish a diagnosis, so they took a history, and the evidence for that is this rather detailed description. It is possible, I think as Dr. Younggren testified earlier, that this information may have been given to them by someone else, but my reading of it suggests to me that someone interviewed Witness A as one would normally do in a clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: What is the purpose of doing that to begin the treatment?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Well, to make a diagnosis. I mean, in any area of medicine, the best way to find out why someone's come in is to talk to them and ask them what's brought them in, what's wrong, what has happened to them in order to start thinking about diagnoses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And after the diagnosis is made in a place like Medica, according to the documents here, what then is done? What kind of therapy is done? Was there any medical therapy? Was there psychotherapy, talking therapies?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: After a diagnosis is made, a clinician will think about what kind of treatment is recommended. If the therapist is a physician and can prescribe medication, they may do that, and we would call that a medication therapy. Also, talking therapies where -- which, a broad term for saying that you sit and talk to someone to try and find a way of relieving their psychological distress. Many different theories about it, many different schools of talking therapy, but essentially the procedure is to do a verbal exchange with someone. In the document, there is a specific reference to "supportive and therapeutic work." I do not know what they mean by that. In the field in general, supportive psychotherapy is a therapy that tries to build on whatever strengths a person has and help them hold things together by emphasising either their connection to other people, or to support them and also to try and minimise the thoughts and feelings that they may be having that are causing them distress, reassuring them, making them feel safe by having them start to talk about what's gone on, what's happened. "Therapeutic work," the term in here indicates to me that the therapists were engaging in some talking relationship to Witness A with the goal of relieving distress. I personally wouldn't know how else to interpret the term "therapeutic work."

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Was there an effect of talking-based therapies on the recitation of traumatic events by chronic PTSD victims?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: A researcher named Dr. Foa has actually examined this question in women who have been raped. She has actually studied the impact of doing a form of talking therapy on how people describe their experiences. She was not interested in examining the question of whether or not memories for trauma change. So in reading her study it's important not to overread information that's not there. What is in her study is evidence that the way people tell their story changes significantly. What I mean by that is, they often begin with fragments, bits and pieces of a story that don't hold together, and they search for a way of organising the information and adding detail and filling things in so that there is more of a story over time. Foa recognises that this means that inconsistencies in the narrative will emerge because people drop out some elements and they add new elements. My understanding of her research is that she is someone who has not said a lot about the idea of whether or not memories for trauma change, but now knowing what we know from three published studies on the fact that people with PTSD change what they say they've either personally experienced or the symptoms of PTSD, I understand that data now, I believe more completely, to show that when people are in therapy, their story changes significantly, and that what they report several weeks after being in therapy or after several sessions may be very different from what they said early on. I admit, I would never know which aspect of a story was true or at which point in time it would be any more accurate. But in her research, and in the research there's a nice article by Dr. Bessel van der Kolk where people have recognised that when we're making memories under highly stressful life-threatening experiences, the memories are not well-organised, that it's really fragmented, and I think people in the field are beginning to recognise that we've made some assumptions in our work that may not, in fact, be true. Our assumption has been that people recorded these photographic images, that they never forget, and that's clearly not the case. So when someone engages in therapy, I would expect that there's a couple of possibilities: Their story will change and they may become much more inconsistent over time. I measure consistency as comparing what the person said at one point in time to another point in time. It's also possible that they would become more consistent over time as they find a comfortable way of telling their story. The goal in therapy is not fact-finding. I mean, as a clinician, the goal in therapy is to try and help someone feel relief, to make them feel less pain and suffering. If a person comes into the clinic and tells a story that then they're more comfortable with, a therapist accepts that story because the goal is relief, not creating more distress. So the story could become consistent and stay the same over time and simply be a reflection of the fact that the person has become more comfortable. I would like to give you one example, if I may, about how a story may change? Someone may have experienced a rape. A woman may come in and say, "I went on a date and I was raped." In interviewing the woman, she may say that she feels responsible or she may say that she feels she was too provocative on the date, maybe her dress was too low or it was inappropriate, and she may say, "I feel guilty. It's my fault." I should be clear, not every patient may say this. And the therapist would work with the patient to help them shift that kind of thinking because the person's distressed. And at the end of the therapy, the patient may say, "You know, it wasn't my fault at all. Whether or not I wore such and such a dress does not justify what this other person did to me. In fact, my dress was not suggestive, it was not provocative, and this person was responsible for containing their own behaviour." So there can be a dramatic shift in not only how they interpret what happened but how they perceive what happened. Once again, the goal is to help people find relief. The therapist doesn't say, "Could you bring me in the dress and I'll decide if it's provocative." You know, if we don't do that -- our goal is to help people get better. But the account, the thinking and feeling about the account can change dramatically. Actually, we count on that as a therapist. I really hope that people find a new way of feeling and thinking about things to get on with their life, to feel better.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have about another 20, 25 minutes of testimony from the doctor before we're completed. Should we break for lunch, or whatever the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's time to break off for lunch, and we shall resume the afternoon sitting at 14.30 hours. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Defence is continuing with Dr. Morgan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Pardon the interruption, Your Honours. We are joined in court at this point in time by an intern lady who is working with our team and -- in the Tribunal. This is Suellen Ratliff. She is seated at the back of court. We hope Your Honours would have no objection to her remaining during the proceedings. I understand my friend has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Obliged, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: At this point in time, we're going to ask the witness to discuss the testimony of Witness A in terms of the tests that he has conducted and has testified here today about. To that extent, I think because it does relate to her testimony, we might want to consider going into a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we should go into closed session -- or private session, as called by the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: As long as the TV camera isn't on the boards. We have some five boards behind the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which may be demonstrated during the testimony of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In that case then, we'll close the blinds. Closed session then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: (Open session).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are in open session. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm obliged. Thank you, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Morgan, I believe there have been essentially four articles that have emerged from the Desert Storm study, is that correct, that have been printed except for the last one?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: You'd have to refresh me on which four you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Well, sir -- yes, I do have copies for the Court and for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: That, Dr. Morgan, is, I believe, the first result or the preliminary report from the Desert Storm research; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: The document I have in front of me does appear to be a copy of our first published study on the Desert Storm veterans, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Presumably Dr. Southwick is the gentleman you referred to earlier, I believe, your boss; yes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And the Andrew Morgan M.D. there is yourself, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: That is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. In that particular report, the initial method was described involving some 84 National Guards reservists; is that so?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Sir, shortly after that -- I say "shortly," two years later, there was a two-year follow-up study; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 8 Prosecution Exhibit number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: So, Dr. Morgan, we now see the two-year follow-up, and I believe the method is then relating to 62 National Guards people, and would that be, in fact, simply that you had had a loss of people between the two points?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Oh, naturally. Longitudinal studies, you expect each year to lose subjects, and most people assume that, as you go over time, fewer people will be involved in a study. It's well-known in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And therefore, sir, presumably, to follow that line, when you include it with an article in February 1997, which was a consistency of memory article relating to that study overall, you referred to 59 National Guards reservists. Were those just the 59 people who were consistent to your study throughout at that point?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Those 59 individuals would have been people who had participated in the study that we had data -- those were people who had completed the data questionnaires at each of those time points.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: So what you're saying that, in fact, as a result, 59 in total completed both questionnaires at both points in time; yeah?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: For this paper, yes. This paper reports on the data from 59 people from both of those time points, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Did you deploy any other questionnaire than your own 19-question document? Did you deploy that on the first occasion, at one month, any other form of scale?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, there were additional scales.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Which did you apply on that occasion, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Well, I think it's mentioned in the first publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Could you perhaps remind us, please?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I think I'd prefer to read it to you, if you'd like? I don't want to misquote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: The questionnaire included a PTSD symptom scale based on DSM IIIR criteria for Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. Subjects rated the following 17 DSM IIIR criteria for PTSD. They rated the following 17 DSM IIIR symptoms, and these are taken from DSM IIIR: intrusive memories, nightmares, flashbacks, feeling worse with war reminders, avoidance of thinking about the war, avoidance of war reminders, amnesia with respect to war --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness read slowly, please?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: -- decreased interest, feeling cut off from other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you read slowly for the interpreters, please?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: All right. Feeling less strongly about things, feeling numb, sleep disturbance, irritability, decreased concentration, being watchful or on guard, increased startle -- or increased startle response, excuse me, and reactivity toward reminders. Symptoms were analysed as individual items and as parts of the three symptom clusters and the degree -- the three symptom clusters I mentioned earlier: re-experiencing, avoidance, and hyperarousal. The degree of severity of each symptom during the preceding month was rated on a scale on which zero equals none, one equals slight, two equals moderate, three equals considerable, and four equals extreme. A total PTSD score was calculated by summing the ratings for each symptom. The end -- allowing for a total possible score of 68. The independence of time, time one versus time two, and symptom severity, a rating of less than two versus a rating of two or higher, was tested using matched pairs chi squared analyses for each of the 17 items. The next section talks about the Mississippi scale. If you want me to read it in detail, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: No, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: It's kind of slow, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: What I would like, if you will be so kind, is to say, did you -- to confirm whether you actually applied the Mississippi scale in that particular study?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I think it's obvious. We report on the findings in all of our papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Did you also apply another scale then, the Combat Experience Scale?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, we did. It's stated right in the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Did you apply all three of those scales at each stage of your research?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: The Mississippi, the Desert Storm Trauma Questionnaire, and the Combat Exposure Scale were applied certainly at the one-month time point and the two-year time point and at the six-year time point. At the six-month time point, there were a certain number of subjects who did not receive the Combat Exposure Scale and therefore they were not included in the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Now, you state that you used a 19-item questionnaire of your own; that is correct? The Desert Storm questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And how many of the questions in that related to what would be termed "directly experienced trauma" in terms of being the direct victim of an event or directly involved in?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Well, our research group had to come to a consensus on that and -- you know, as a research group, people would agree that a certain number of the items were unmistakably objective, such as sitting with the dying, being injured, seeing someone killed, and that a certain number of items, there would be some flexibility around subjective perception, like threatened personal safety. I really can't tell you off the top of my head how we actually rated each item. It would be unfair.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And I understand that the questionnaire essentially would pose such questions. Let us take an example of whether one had been in an aeroplane over enemy air space, something of that nature; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes. They flew to the Gulf.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: As opposed to one where: Have you ever been shot down in an aeroplane?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yeah, I believe one item is: Did the aeroplane receive enemy fire?

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: You say, obviously, it seems from the approach you use, it was a "Yes"-"No" situation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I think I stated before it's "Yes," "No," and they had an opportunity to indicate the number of times for each item.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Number of times. That was not, though, quite clearly, the methodology was not to take a kind of interview, a witness statement, and actually get all the surrounding facts relating to an event at that stage; that would be correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: We weren't evaluating witnesses, we were interviewing veterans coming back from a war zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: When you got to the six-year study, I believe you referred to having some 32 participants remaining in the exercise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: For the consistency of memory at six years, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And I believe you described the sample group at -- in one part of the report it says 27 men and 7 women. I don't think that adds up to 30 but ...

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I wouldn't know without looking back at the paper, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I could -- we can show you that, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I'm just wondering, Dr. Morgan, if there is any statistical significance why the figures don't appear to add up precisely?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, there would be, and by looking at the statistical analyses, it's obvious that the paragraph under "Methods" has a misstatement in it about the number of women. The statistical analyses, from that you can derive the number of people in the subject. As I say, this is a paper that is currently in review, and those kinds of typographical errors in a paper are what are caught by editors. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Now, I understand, if I understand correctly, that at the two-year point, when you used the Mississippi scale -- and believe me, sir, I'm no expert in these matters -- but you made a reference to the changes in responses in the questionnaire being "not statistically significant." Was that a correct observation in relation -- on my part, is that a correct observation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: You're asking me whether or not the --

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I believe that you stated that the differences shown on the Mississippi scale at the two-year point -- one of your --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Oh, in the two-year paper is what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: The two-year paper, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: You actually refer that it was not statistically significant, the changes measured on that scale; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I will check the findings right now on the paper. Actually, in our second-year paper, the Mississippi scale score did increase significantly over time, and that's on page 1153 of the publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Morgan, how many subjects exhibited or were qualified for a diagnosis of chronic PTSD at the point of your second year, the two-year survey?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I believe we've stated that as well in the paper. Depending on which criteria are used, and you'll notice at one point we use the criteria on the PTSD symptoms scale and we also provide the information as measured by the Mississippi scale. We do both because one of the questions in our field and one of the jobs at the National Centre is to establish criteria for PTSD, and this paper is written to inform about that, which is why we provide different ways of making the diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: But in point of fact, just how many people was it at that point out of your sample who still had PTSD?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I think -- I can read it out loud or you can, if you'd like. When a cut-off score of 89 was used on the Mississippi scale, in the second-year paper, we had two subjects who met criteria at one month for Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. In addition to those two subjects, two more met criteria for PTSD at six months. These four and two more met criteria for PTSD at two years. So when you add them up, it matches the prevalence in the general population of between 9 and 10 per cent of the total sample which is a nice reminder that the paper is a reliable reflection of both the prevalence of PTSD in a natural group and supports the validity of our findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Sir, how many people remained in -- were PTSD sufferers at the six-year point?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: At the six-year time point, out of the subjects that we saw, I'm aware of three people who met full criteria for PTSD, and once again, three out of 30 to 32 subjects -- re-check the data -- in between 9 and 10 per cent, once again, a very accurate reflection of what we find in the population. I should point out, so it's not misinterpreted, we looked at the full continuum, and so did Dr. Roemer in her study of 460 subjects, and the findings are, in fact, the same. The more symptoms of PTSD, the more inconsistencies, and the individuals with PTSD had the most inconsistencies. The three subjects in our six-year study were the three individuals who change nearly every response on their questionnaire. So I would caution people from paying attention to small numbers. These are numbers in people we've evaluated consistently over time and it's now been replicated in larger studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Suffice it to say for the purposes of the conclusions subsequently drawn in these studies, we do have a variation in the sample group, do we not, sir, and, in fact, from the original 84 we start with, we ended up with 32; is that broadly fair to say?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: No, it would not be scientifically fair to say at all. In longitudinal samples, you have a representative sample and you submit it to peer review and your peers let you know whether or not it is a valid representation of the data. They've been published. People accept our data. We know what we're doing. I mean, I think people who don't understand that just don't understand this kind of research. I don't know what else to say except that anyone who does longitudinal studies should expect to see half their subjects have left the study within four years. If you don't see that when you evaluate a paper, you need to ask a question about what did they do? People have documented this kind of a finding over the last 20 in years in longitudinal research.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: There is one thing however, to move on. You have stated throughout it's a question of consistency; is that right? It's just consistency.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: That's precisely what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: This is consistency of the memory. Is it not true -- sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: It's consistency of reported memory, and I believe I tried to be very clear on that this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Indeed. And I'm moving on to that very point because is it not so you conceded in your studies that the reliability and validity of the questionnaire in factual terms was never established or verified; is that so?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: For the Desert Storm trauma questionnaire, that is true. For the War Stress questionnaire, that is not true. Neither is it true for the Combat Exposure Scale which are well-validated. The good news is that they all match, the percentages are the same, and people in the field of PTSD are content with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And that, sir, obviously, on the issue of consistency. But as regards the issue of the factual accuracy of a human memory, you could not say that that model of yours tested factual accuracy.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I know of no model in the world that can directly measure what anyone knows in their mind. Perhaps startle is the closest you can get. But I know of no way of measuring what people actually remember. People can misstate, they can forget, they can be mistaken, they can lie, they can do all sorts of things. I said this morning I think that apart from other objective independent evidence like photographs, hard data that can't be shifted, consistency of reported memory is all anyone has ever measured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: But I believe you've actually stated in your research, did you not, Doctor, that the self-rated questionnaire, as I believe you called it, you deemed to have its limitations in that respect.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's why I was delighted to see Carol North's study and I've also seen a study by Dr. Goodman who used direct interviews with people and found highly similar results. People were inconsistent whether they filled out a form or whether they were directly interviewed and asked about their symptoms. But, absolutely, anyone who does this research knows that giving people paper and pencil tests is a valid way of measuring data, but when you can, you get a direct interview. It's not always possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I believe you did precisely that to the extent of interviewing your subjects at the six-year point; is that correct, Dr. Morgan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Am I correct in suggesting to you, sir, that one method that is approved of in such research is the use of what they call a blind interviewer, i.e. someone who is not involved in the research; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Is that a preferred and approved way of trying to be as impartial and even-handed as possible in the research?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and we've indicated that in our paper. Dr. Steven Southwick actually interviewed the other half of the subjects, and we had a third person, a Dr. Goldstein, independently rate the record of our interviews with the subjects and make her evaluation on the data. So we did just that. We took turns interviewing people, we did not compare our notes, and we had a third party evaluate them. It's the best way to do the research.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: There were, I believe, certain responses that you received in relation to the reasons for an apparent inconsistency of memory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: We had people tell us why they thought their answers changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And I believe you've disclosed in your work that one person made a change of his response because of basically his interpretation of the word "friends" or "friend," whether the person or persons killed would be a friend; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I believe I also mentioned that this morning in testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Yes, indeed you did, sir. I believe another response was to do with the impression of being close to enemy lines; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: There is a statement in our paper about being close to enemy lines, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I believe there, sir, the gentleman, in civilian life, commuted that distance daily and thought, in fact, it was quite a long way but --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: But he still remembered quite clearly as a fact, did he not, the presence of the enemy lines? They had been there.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: You know, that was the question we had when we sat with him, and we tried to get at that, and what he said, and I believe it is in the paper, he said, "Well, we were close to enemy lines, 30 miles is close when it's the enemy, but I drive 30 miles to work every day, so that's a long way."

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Exactly, sir. And, in fact, therefore he was working, was he not, from a memory that recalled two salient facts: one was the fact of enemy lines and the other was the fact they were 30 miles away?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Oh, I don't know. I actually put in the paper as well that the explanations the subjects gave us would include that possibility, but more importantly, we concluded that none of the explanations may be true, and that's because people, when you confront them with inconsistencies in their reports, get anxious, they get upset. We found in our subjects, people got defensive and they would say things like, "Well, that's not my handwriting. I didn't do this." And we would say, "Well, is it your handwriting?" And they would then say "Yes." And so we suggest in our paper that one possibility for their answers is that they feel they have to come up with an answer. They need to find something that makes sense to make it logically consistent. We concluded at the end of our paper that most of the subjects were unable to be satisfied with their responses, and we concluded that sometimes maybe the pressure or the demand characteristic, is how we refer to it in scientific studies, that the pressures on a person sitting with someone like a doctor or a scientist, that that sort of -- that pressure influences them to come up with something, and rather than say, "You know, I don't know," or "I lied" or "I'm completely inconsistent," they would come up with some meaningful explanation. So we try to emphasise in our paper that we, in fact, don't know if any of the explanations people gave us were true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Morgan, it seems rather strange, though, that the people, simply for assisting you in a psychological research, feel so threatened if taken to task over a response? Was there anything about the circumstances that would be threatening to them?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: We were not aware of anything that would be threatening to them, but most researchers do agree that for an individual to come in and meet scientists, there may be demand characteristics, just like someone coming in, meeting an attorney, meeting a judge, meeting a police officer, it isn't their sort of everyday experience, and we had to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I apologise, but this really is too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please be slower. There is interpretation that has to go on.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So we had to consider that the explanations were possible explanations but perhaps not true explanations of our data.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: But equally then, if one is going to speculate in that direction, one can speculate the other way, that they were simple, logical, truthful responses in the sense of accuracy?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: You know, our subjects didn't agree with us on that, but that is a possible way of interpreting the data. It's harder when we looked at the items about people being injured and shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Well, I will quote one last example of that which I believe was a man who corrected his response about seeing a woman killed --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: -- because he said what really happened was he heard the blast and then moments later saw the body and associated the two. Would that not be a very logical and sensible response?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: You're referring to the fellow who said he had seen a photograph later and then said --

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: There's an example in our paper of a fellow who believed he had seen the nurse in the unit killed and then he said, "I couldn't have seen it because I heard the blast and then saw the body," and he later believed that he had, in fact, seen her.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll verify that point, Dr. Morgan.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I don't know which one you're referring to. I'd have to look and you can show me in the paper, but I know in our paper there's the example of the fellow who believed he had seen someone killed and later said it was because he had seen a photograph and that he had -- he had been around the explosion but, in fact, he did not see her. He had seen her body later. He came to believe that the photograph of her, the picture in his head, he said, was the picture in the photograph. That was striking to us, because we had understood from post-event information studies that this phenomenon occurs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Well, if I can move on from that point, Dr. Morgan, we can verify that. Pardon the interruptions, Your Honours. I'm quoting from your own six-year study here. It is page 2079.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: The second paragraph down says, "I must have focused on the word 'seen.' I must have taken that to mean I actually saw her the moment she died. I only heard the blast then saw her a few seconds afterward. I guess it all depends on what you mean by 'seen.'"

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes. I see where you are. And the question was?

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Again, was that not very probably or possibly a perfectly logical and actual -- accuracy memory based response from somebody?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I believe that it's not a measure of accuracy. It does seem to demonstrate logic on the part of the subject, but, in fact, the subject wasn't pleased with the answer. They weren't sure of their answers. These are ways they were trying to come to grips with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I believe you subsequently commented in your six-year article, Dr. Morgan, that you recommended a closer focus on the use of words in future research to avoid these problems?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Oh, yes. And Dr. Goodman has recommended the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: So isn't it, therefore -- sorry. Isn't it, therefore, possibly the tools that have caused the problem there? There have been misimpressions from the nature of questions asked?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Well, I think in our paper and in Dr. Roemer's paper we do raise that issue for our field in trauma studies, that the way we assess people may influence the way they answer, and we believe that's very similar across settings. However, the data from Dr. North is not -- was done with direct interviews, and she too found significant inconsistencies, people denying their -- in fact, their illness, the symptoms, nightmares and illness that are supposed to be indelible of their traumatic event. So I think taken together, the studies are not supportive of the idea that this is a problem with questionnaires. In doing research in the field, we would like to improve questionnaires. We always like to improve techniques. Medicine is like that. We always like to improve how we work with people in diagnosing them, but it's not an explanation for the data that's held up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Morgan, did you make any observation at the end of your studies relating to the responses of healthy, non-treatment seeking individuals?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And what was your general view as to the presence of any inconsistency amongst such people?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Our view is that a single source of information for reported memory is not scientifically reliable independent of external corroborating evidence, and I -- and I believe that we stress that, which is why we encourage people to remember this is not -- this is not about recovered memory, this is about consistency of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Indeed so. It's about consistency of reporting. And I believe you did indicate that inconsistency is also pretty common amongst people without PTSD, normal, healthy people?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I think that's evident in the paper, in that the PTSD people did it significantly more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Now, turning to the question of accuracy of memory, accuracy is, indeed, is it not, a different dimension of memory to that of consistency?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: People have argued that this is. I do not know, in fact, whether or not that is demonstrated in the field of PTSD.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: But it's generally a matter of human memory, that accuracy is separate element of memory compared to ability for completeness or for consistency?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I need to be specific. Accuracy is a term that I know to be associated with a neurologic test, like a memory test, where a person is presented with specific information against which their responses can be compared, and investigators feel comfortable saying you're accurate or not, if you get the items. However, apart from a neurologic test in word recall, I do not know of a way to assess accuracy for traumatic events.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Let us look, if we can, at the situation of people who do suffer from PTSD. I believe under DSM IV, this is the sort of diagnostic criteria, is it not true that it's the development of characteristic symptoms following exposure to an extreme traumatic stressor? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to quote it verbatim, but if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I can show you a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I would agree with the statement, but I'd like to make sure it's being quoted correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And included in that diagnosis, sir, in DSM IV, they include such things as direct personal experience of an event. Is that one of things that can happen?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: In DSM IV, one of the two prongs for the traumatic event is that the individual must be exposed to something that is personally threatening, threatening to their personal integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And as a matter of interest of your studies, sir -- Dr. Morgan, did you not find that the scores relating to those subjected to direct stress or direct trauma were, in fact, a little more consistent than those who suffered indirect trauma when you compared the studies in your Desert Storm research?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: No. I think what we reported is that people with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder made many more changes in their report. They were more inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Then let me put it another way. Did you see more consistency in responses in relation generally to direct trauma as opposed to the indirect trauma across people generally?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I'm a little confused by your question, because I do not recall, in any of our papers, making a distinction of that kind in the statistical analyses or reporting in that way. If you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I don't think it was --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: -- want to refresh my memory, but we didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I don't think it was an analytical conclusion. I'm saying was it that the scores in relation to the direct traumas indicated perhaps a greater consistency than in respect of the indirect traumas?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Once again, I'm saying we didn't -- we didn't compare direct and indirect statistically, so it would be impossible to affirm or negate what you're saying. We showed that the more trauma symptoms they had the more inconsistent they were, the more sicker they were, the more changes in their report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Now, if we move on then to traumatic events, Dr. Morgan.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: When other studies in connection with the business of traumatic memory as such --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I described four of them this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And would that be -- include such things -- would that be including the studies of John Yuille and the events of impact? You're familiar with that, sir, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Is it not true that in 1986 John Yuille and others actually dealt with a real life event of a shoot-out at a gun store, I believe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection of his study, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I will verify it to you later, sir, but I believe they carried out interviews of the exact -- the actual witnesses to this event, and researchers did so five or six months after the event, so they've been police interviewed and researched. Is that, to your recollection, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Once again, I'd have to look at the study directly. It's not a study on Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, or memory in people with post traumatic stress, so it hasn't been relevant to the work we've been doing, but I would review it for you if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Well, if I could just give you some detail, sir, and obviously we will produce this to you in fullness of time to verify. If I would suggest to you, sir, that there was, in fact, something like a 60 per cent increase in additional information observed six months after the event?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: You mean, they went from poor to slightly better.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I'm saying that at this stage, sir, it was 560 [stenographer error] per cent increase in information.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Relevant to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: My friend for the Defence indicates there may be a problem on the transcript. It says 560.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you did say 60 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Morgan, if I could just suggest this to you, and I will provide you with the article in due course, that this was new information on the part of witnesses in respect of the events of the robbery they witnessed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And apparently accuracy rates were very high, between 85 and 90 per cent, for the factual information recalled. And this included details of the action, which I believe were about 82 per cent, descriptions of the robbers at 76 per cent and so forth?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: So about 1 in 4 were not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: In respect of --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: You said 76 per cent, so approximately 25 per cent, 1 in 4, of the description were is inaccurate. That's actually like what I reported this morning, that inaccuracies look to be in the range of 30 to 40 per cent on the yes to no, and no to yes changes. But once again that, to my knowledge, and I will review it later if you'll give me the paper, the assessment time points are not identical. They're not given the same instrument. So it's not a controlled study. And, two, it's not a study of people with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. So it's really not relevant to what I presented this morning, but if you give me the paper I'd be happy to critically review it. It's been reviewed and summarised in -- well, in Dr. Charney's book, Neurobiological Consequences of Stress.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Morgan, the -- is it not true that there is a body of opinion that the emotionally experienced memory is perhaps more vividly encoded than other memories of a more normal learning process?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes. There's -- there's substantial evidence from animals and from people that we remember emotionally meaningful things better than neutral things, and I think, as I said this morning, it sort of makes sense if you're threatened by something, your body produces adrenaline. We know adrenaline helps our memory. When people get overwhelmed in life-threatening events the stress hormones are no longer helpful and they disrupt memory. But I think everyone knows, from their own personal life experience, they remember a party that was fun. They remember an unpleasant argument with someone. So they remember unpleasant things more than neutral things. Where they left paper clips this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Indeed. And on the basis, therefore, that this might be a stronger memory, would it be more likely to be a more enduring memory?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Well, we all know that's not true. That, in fact, was our assumption when we began our studies. We had actually predicted that the memories in the veterans, and so did Dr. Roemer and Dr. North, predicted that people's memories for these life-threatening events, people getting killed beside them, bombs blowing up, people shooting other people in front of them, that those would not change. And in fact, in her study, and our study and Carol North's, people's reports change. We've had to rethink what we think the gist of a memory is. The major event that's threatening to people changes in their report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Morgan, you've just referred to the expression "gist." What do you mean by that, what definition?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: It's not a scientific term, in my view, because it's imprecise. I know that it is used as a layman's term for people generally implying, "You got the main intent of my message."
