Now, in our studies, if what we mean by gist is that our subjects knew they went to the Gulf War, then the gist was correct. If we wanted to say that people knew they'd been in that shoot-out in Texas, then the gist was correct. However, if we're going to say that the gist is, "Did you or did you not see somebody injured or shot or killed," we know for a fact those items change. The gist, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: You are aware, sir, that there is, again, a body of study that would indicate that gist is the more memorable than periphery detail? Would you agree with that proposition at all?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I am aware of a body of study that cannot be legitimately related to studies in Post Traumatic Stress Disorder where gist is referred to, and I'm speaking of the literature on recovered memory. That literature cannot be scientifically compared to literature on Post Traumatic Stress Disorder for this reason: According to DSM IV, to make a diagnosis of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, you have to first establish a traumatic event. After establishing the traumatic event by the person's report, you make a diagnosis based on symptoms that are present. In the field of recovered memory, individuals are assessed by therapists, who complain of symptoms and who work backwards from those symptoms and go in search of a trauma that the patient can't remember, and they search until they find one. We call that recall bias, retrospective bias. It is not a scientifically valid way of doing research these days, and looking at the effects of stress on the brain and understanding what we know about brain functioning. I am aware that many people would like to compare these two fields. At the National Centre -- the National Centre is the premier institution in the United States and the international system. It is a large group of investigators. The National Centre and the International Society for Traumatic Stress Studies are both clear. The recovered memory issue is not to be compared with the research and our understanding --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We apologise. This is too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please speak slowly. Too fast for interpreters.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I think this does a disservice to research in Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, and it does disservice to people suffering from Post Traumatic Stress Disorder to equate the two. And I don't want to give the Court the impression that these studies that purportedly show that memory for recovered memories, whether it's ritual satanic abuse or whatever, alien abductions, whatever, I wouldn't want the Court to have the impression that that is considered in the same realm of science as the work we do with victims of rape, you know, victims of trauma, victims of war. That's why I feel very strongly about that. Part of our mission is education from the National Centre, and there has been a vigorous debate in the United States, in the court systems, over this recovered memory debate, and we really owe it to the public to say these are apples and oranges, two different kinds of things. People who know they've been traumatised, they've known that they've been traumatised and who are sick as a result of that trauma. We are not talking about people who say, "Well, I feel ill," and then meet with the therapist and other time suddenly discover that horrible things they never ever remembered before had occurred to them in childhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Morgan, you made reference at the outset of your last remarks about the sort of flashbulb situation of a traumatic memory. Now, for those who have tested that theory, are you aware of the areas in which they found any inconsistency or loss of recall of accuracy in relation to those events? Are you aware of that, sir, or not? You can answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Very well. Let me put it this way: The flashbulb research took place generally in respect of very notable historical public events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I mentioned this morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: -- the assassination of John F. Kennedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Indeed. John F. Kennedy, the Challenger disaster, I believe.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I believe the death of the Premier in Sweden on one -- was one study as well--

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I referred to that. Christensen's study as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Is it not true that in respect of those kinds of memories, whatever the subsequent inconsistency, the fact is people still remembered the event? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Once again, it depends what you mean by the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: The event. If we take the assassination of John Kennedy --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: It's everything to my answer. If you phone someone back up and say, "You're in our study because we're asking you about the assassination of JFK or the Challenger," they're reminded of the event in question. But we can't forget the gist of the study. The gist of the study reminds them what you're going to ask about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Is it not true that those studies showed that they might have remembered the event and the place, whereas they would not remember necessarily the circumstances they were in when they heard the news? That's what I'm trying to get at.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I am aware that many of the subjects were unable to report where they were and what they were doing, and were significantly inconsistent. I am aware that a number of subjects were consistent. I'm also aware that the authors of those studies concluded that, in fact, they didn't support the notion of flashbulb memories, and one author went so far as to then redefine what a flashbulb memory would be. They decided 60 per cent was good enough. A hundred per cent down to 60 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Morgan, is it true that people who suffer PTSD sometimes suffer from a delayed recovery of their memories?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: In my experience, I have never found that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: So you would expect, in the case of PTSD, the person would have continuing memory, would you, from shortly after the event?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Based on what we know from combat veterans, from rape victims, from victims of natural disasters, we have generally found that people know they were in a war zone, they know they had a rape, and they have not reported extended periods of amnesia for those events. Although, I have treated veterans who believed they were in Vietnam and remembered their experiences, and we have now been informed by the government that they were not, in fact, deployed to Vietnam. So they, in fact, have memories for traumatic events that could not have occurred in Vietnam. So the consistency of reporting trauma is not a measure of accuracy, it's a reflection of how sick people feel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Presumably by diagnosing those symptoms and the fact that these people are sick, they have clearly undergone a trauma.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: That's putting the cart before the horse. We don't reason backwards and say since they have symptoms they must have been traumatised, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: If you have researched somebody and made the diagnosis that they have Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, is it not logical that there must obviously have been the presence of the stress or trauma?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: It does depend on the clinician. No. At the National Centre, you have to verify now that a person has been deployed in the army theatre where they were deployed. In fact, very little additional information is often available in military records. For rape victims who come in, since it's a clinic, we don't ask the rape victim to provide evidence of where they were raped, and we do not ask them to provide evidence that they were raped. Since it's a clinic, we take that at face value, and I think as was explained yesterday and by me this morning, the therapeutic perspective is we accept people how they come into the clinic. It's different than how you do scientific studies on memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: On that basis, sir, you would say obviously you would let them relay to you what they say they recall of the rape?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: As a clinician?

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: You let them say what they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Exactly. And, therefore, if -- so if somebody comes in and gives that account, you will simply accept that as being their memories at that time? I presume that's fair to say.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: We accept what the patient says and proceed from there for therapy. We don't have to believe that it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And as you say, the studies that you have conducted generally do not give any insight into accuracy other than you've referred to an indirect insight into accuracy?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I stated earlier that consist -- studying consistency provides an indirect and yet limited way of viewing accuracy. I say that because there are times when people give two diametrically opposed reports. The example, I think it was mentioned yesterday, is -- the reference was, was Mr. Furundzija tall and dark or short and blonde? Can't be both. Now, I don't know -- now that I've seen him he looks tall and dark, but I didn't know that reading documents, so I would have no idea which account or description was accurate. I would know they weren't consistent, and would I say to myself, "Can't be both, it's possible that he's neither. He could be red haired." So in that sense, consistency is a role of indirectly getting an impression of accuracy. But it -- I know of no method for measuring accuracy in every day life, in the real world situation for studying trauma.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Indeed. Dr. Morgan, certain studies and authorities supplied to us, initially as a basis for your testimony, included some of those of Dr. Loftus and others, and one of those was, I believe, a laboratory experiment in respect of accuracy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I don't know to what you're referring. I didn't turn in any references by Dr. Loftus, so I'm not sure what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I can ask you another way then Dr. Morgan. Are you aware of the Loftus and Burns study of 1990 -- I'm sorry, 1982, based on a robbery scenario?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: You'd have to show me the study. Once again, Dr. Loftus's work has not been about Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, and it has not been about the nature of memory in people with PTSD, so I would have to review a paper before to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, we've reached our break time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, Ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we break for this afternoon, I would wish to announce that tomorrow the proceedings will start at 10.30, because the Trial Chamber is involved in other cases from 9.00 hours on. So these proceedings will start tomorrow at 10.30 hours. So we will break for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you please wrap up? I wonder how long you have to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I can't be certain. I could imagine we would probably be the better part of another half to three-quarters of an hour minimum, I'm sorry to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We would appreciate it if you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I will do my level best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Morgan, I mentioned a study just before the break, but I do not propose to put that to you now, save us a little time. Prior to that, we were talking -- I talked briefly about emotional memories and memories for traumatic events. Now, if you absent Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, it would be true to say, would it not, that such memories would tend to be stronger and more positively retained; is that so?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: It's generally agreed that in humans, they will remember emotional things better than neutral things; that is not to say that memory for an overwhelming event will be remembered better than a memory for a non-life-threatening traumatic event. People I think in general know that some stress enhances performance. For example, an athlete preparing for a game may have an increase in adrenaline or someone performing on a test may have an increase in adrenaline and be able to pay more attention and do better in the sport or on a test or remember something. But we know clearly from 50 years of research, since Canon's work in the early part of the century, that it's a curve in that as stress increases, performance is enhanced; but as stress gets higher and higher and higher, performance diminishes. Common experience might be being too stressed out. People then start not to pay attention if a test gets too stressful or if a competition gets too overwhelming. I think the common viewing of that, like on television, would be watching the Olympics and seeing very fine athletes who have done that performance thousands of times but who arrive at the competition and perhaps can't do the behaviour they've been training to do, they can't get it right, and in the realm of sports psychology, people are agreed that that's because people differ in their ability to manage the stress under -- to manage the stress of the competition and performance falls off. So that in everyday life, there is a relationship that is positive between enhanced performance and an increase in stress, but it is not true that when stress becomes overwhelming that you necessarily see enhanced performance. There are a lot of studies in animals and in people that show, as you increase some stress, people remember things a bit better; but as the stress gets higher, they don't. So it's not what we call a linear relationship, it's not just as stress keeps increasing, you just get better and better and better and better, there's just no end point. It's a curve that kind of looks like an "n" that as stress goes up, performance goes up but then falls away. Memory appears to behave in the same way, that as stress increases slightly, we remember a little better; as it increases more, we don't remember so well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dr. Morgan, you have analysed a number of -- or, sorry, you have reviewed a number of the statements made by the witness in this case; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Yes. And you have seen elements of events repeated over a period of time; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you ask me that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: You have seen elements of certain events that occurred over a period of time set out in those statements?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Can you tell me what you mean by "elements" and then I would know how to answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Various factual incidents, because you've actually compared -- you've made comparison charts from that information.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. I have made comparisons between statements. I do not know if they're facts and I don't want to imply to people that I pretend to know whether they are true or not true. "Elements" is a broad word. I think what I'm comfortable saying is I reviewed the statements and I have noted inconsistencies and there are, obviously, consistencies. Witness A has said all along that she was in captivity, that she suffered rape, that she was held against her will, that she was frightened, that she was sort of frozen and shocked and disoriented. Those are consistent statements. I don't know whether or not they're accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Would such experiences generally qualify as events that would impact heavily on the memory?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Being confronted with a threat of rape --

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Let me take you through. For instance, being seized by a group of armed soldiers, taken and held somewhere; would that be an intense emotion? Would it be like gist? Would it be gist of the story?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Being seized by enemy soldiers would be -- I would reasonably assume that that would be an alarming event. I do not know -- I would want to know from the person seized whether they were alarmed by it --

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you this then -- if we can use a "Yes"-"No" basis? Would you consider it to be, for want of a better word, traumatic for such a woman to be taken into captivity and then stripped of her clothing? Would that be an intense emotional experience?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I think that would fit into a category of a potentially stressful event.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Would the presence of an interrogator in that particular situation be a significant, an intense detail?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I think, once again, that would depend on what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Then if the interrogator added threats to the lives of the children of that person, would that be an intense experience?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Are you asking me if someone says to someone, "I would harm your children --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: In that scenario, would you -- from your experience, would you put that on the side of an intense experience?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I think that reasonably falls into the realm of things that could be Category A events, threatening events.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: In that situation, the person who is held by armed soldiers, interrogated, if they add the threat of, say, genital mutilation with a knife, would that be an additional element that would be again intense?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: That's a possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: A possibility.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Well, those are the things in DSM IV that listed: sexual assaults --

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Would then to suffer repeated rape in such circumstances, would that also be an intense experience?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I would consider that as an intense experience, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: If that took place in front of someone who was also being held, who was acquainted with you, would that add to that tension and trauma?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I don't know if that would add. I think most people would assume that the rape itself would be traumatic and would not know how to answer the question as to whether or not someone was more worried about someone watching while they were getting raped. I think most victims would be concerned with what was happening to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And in those circumstances, sir, would you agree that the potential is there obviously for PTSD?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: There's a potential for PTSD, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And is it not true that the symptoms of PTSD include, quite often, intrusive, recurring memories?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Intrusive, recurring memories are one of the symptoms listed for Post Traumatic Stress Disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And I believe you made a reference earlier about the absence of uncontrollable thoughts denied by the -- pardon me a moment. My learned colleague does advise me that, of course, certain matters were in closed session, and I'm trying to be careful not to step over that boundary without alerting the Chamber, but I don't know if Your Honours feel maybe we are getting close enough to that issue. I will be making some references in due course to the charts as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Well, in that case, then it's safer to be in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think it would be safer to go now, Ma'am. I've kept it to as late as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: "Private session," so called.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm obliged to you for that, Ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: (Open session).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we're in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Obliged, Ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: You've testified to the effect of certain things released in the human body under stress which may affect parts of the brain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I've mentioned only two of a great number of stress hormones; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And of these two stress hormones, you suggest they cause some damage to the hippocampus?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I believe I stated that adrenaline is known to disrupt concentration and attention which are vital to forming memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And if someone -- sorry, please?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I was waiting for the translator. And I also said that the glucocorticoids have been demonstrated to produce cell damage in the hippocampus. I did not mention beta endorphins, e-n-d-o-r-p-h-i-n, it's the body's natural pain-killer, and their effect at reducing memory, and they too are released under conditions of high stress.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And in what kind of studies have these effects been researched?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: In both animal and in human studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And how many studies are human studies?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: For which hormone?

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: I'm no expert in hormones, sir, but the effects of stress generally on memory?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: This is really the focus of several books. To my knowledge, the most comprehensive book to date is edited by Matthew Friedman, Ariel Deutsch and Dennis Charney, and it is called the Neurobiological Consequences of Stress from Normal Adaptation to Post Traumatic Stress Disorder, and it reflects thousands of studies if you count the animal studies and then looking at the human studies, and I would not be able to tell you the exact numbers of studies. I can only mention some of the more famous studies and well-known studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Is one of those well-known studies that of I believe a Dr. Bremner?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Dr. Bremner has actually done more than 30 to 40 studies. I'd have to know to which ones you're referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Would they be the general groups who have been used as your subjects -- or the subjects for that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: The general groups are trauma victims for Dr. Bremner's work. He studies trauma victims, men and women who have Post Traumatic Stress Disorder from adult and childhood trauma.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Would you, sir, not place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, can we move on? We've done too much on general studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I will be through very shortly I can now assure you, Your Honours, I really will.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Was one of those studies that you placed considerable reliance on involving Vietnam veterans? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Once again, Dr. Bremner has done most of his work in Vietnam veterans and in women with sexual assault related PTSD.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Dealing with the Vietnam veteran cases, is it not true that amongst the research group there is a high rate of prior alcohol dependency history?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: It is true that in men with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder from a war zone, many men have a problem with alcohol. Fortunately, the studies looking at the hippocampus in women with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder have taken that factor into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Can I just -- but as for those studies, you would concede, would you, it would be a factor, a potential factor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I will defer to the top journal of science in the world, the journal Science, who published an update, a report for the world on the effects of stress on the brain. It's entitled Why Stress is Bad for Your Brain. Dr. Sapolsky is the author of report in Science, and he and the rest of the science community have accepted the findings of the four published studies -- the four studies that I know are published on hippocampal brain damage in people with PTSD, and that is not counting the three additional studies that are currently in press that have not only replicated the four previous studies but have actually increased our knowledge that the brain damage is much more significant than we had thought. The early studies showed that the hippocampus may be significantly reduced up to 8 per cent in its volume. The new studies that have now been presented at conferences and that are in review show that up to 18 per cent of the hippocampus is damaged. To give a comparison, people who suffer from Alzheimer's disease, a condition well recognised for its disturbances and its effect on the mind, those patients have a 25 per cent reduction in the hippocampus. So that people with Post Traumatic Stress Disorder have at least an 8 per cent reduction. It now appears it may be as high as 18 per cent. But there is no question in the field that these findings are consistent and reliable. So I -- that's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: All right. In conclusion, Dr. Morgan, you -- you stated that in your research you had single-source information; correct? Self-reported, single source?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: As in the case that I've looked at here for the Court --

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: -- we had subjects from whom we obtained multiple reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In other words, you had single people answering the questions. And some of those clearly did have PTSD that was diagnosed; yes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Right. Now, sir, what would you consider the impact of the existence of corroboration when you take it alongside those findings?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: It depends on what kind of corroboration. In our study, we interviewed each of the members of the military units who were deployed to the same places in their respective units. It was not helpful for us to compare their reports to one another, in that they too were inconsistent between one another as well as within their own reports. So it would depend on what kind of corroboration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: But would you say that if anyone is satisfied that there is corroboration in a situation, clearly that would assist in establishing the accuracy and indeed the consistency of memory, but certainly accuracy, would it not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: I think an objective, independent source of corroborative evidence would be essential in trying to evaluate multiple inconsistent reports from an individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: And, in fact, isn't it so that you concluded, sir, your six-year replication -- you concluded that, did you not, with the sentence, "Thus, the current data suggests that inconsistencies in reports of trauma should not automatically imply that a victim..." -- sorry, "... a witness, victim or patient is unreliable." Those are the words?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Oh, yes, indeed, those are the words. And they're there for a very important reason. Dr. Southwick and I worked very hard on the wording of our paper, to prevent people from automatically assuming that because someone has suffered trauma that they're an unreliable witness. However, we -- and we wanted to remind people that we were not interested in getting into the recovered memory debate. We felt we went to great lengths at the end of our paper to keep clinicians, first of all, from using inconsistent reports against their own patients. We're actually concerned that people may misinterpret our findings and then say to patients, "You're lying," or, "You're wrong." And we believe that that would be harmful in a clinic setting to a patient. So in our paper we said we do not want these findings to be automatically applied to a courtroom setting. We would hope that people would have other evidence other than inconsistent reports, and that's why we stated it very carefully and at the end of our paper. Our paper is most likely to be coming out in a journal that's read by clinicians, not only research scientists, and we don't think that they should use the inconsistencies to doubt their patients or to convey doubt and lack of trust in the patients. So I really agree with the statement, and I don't think anyone should be automatically, without looking at all evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Finally, sir --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: -- be rejected as a patient or as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Finally, Dr. Morgan, did you not express studies, generally at this stage, you felt were not, in fact, ready for court related use? Is that correct? Could you just answer yes or no to that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: It would not be truthful answer if I answer yes or no, but I can answer yes or no. I would prefer not to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: Very well, sir. I'm happy with that. I have no further questions, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. I suppose the Defence will want to re-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DAVIDSON
utterances.text: We have nothing on redirect. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The Court has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Dr. Morgan, I have one or two questions which are naive, of course, naive questions. I am trained in law and have no knowledge of psychology or psychiatry, so I apologise for asking naive questions. May I refer you to Exhibit D24, which you should have in front of you. D24, it's the Medica report.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes, the Medica document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, the Medica document. Now, it is clear from this document that it consists of two parts. One is page 1, the reply of the Medica centre.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It's a two-page report. Then as a sort of attachment we may read the three reports made respectively on the 24th of December, '93, 31st of December, '93 and 11th of July, '95.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES ALEXANDER MORGAN III
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Now, if I read this document, particularly in the first document, "Reply", I have the feeling, and I wonder whether this is correct, that in a way it was only in '98, when this reply was drafted and sent to us, that Witness A was formally diagnosed with PTSD, and this diagnosis was based, if I read this document correctly, on the reports prepared in '93, '93 and '95, because actually, on the first page, they clearly say, "We feel that the Witness A was suffering of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder -- Post Traumatic Stress Syndrome on the report based in '93, and for this purpose ...", they go on to say, "... we have underlined, in the report of 24th of December, '93 the relevant sentences," which in a way disclose symptoms of this syndrome. We can see them on page 3. "She was released from the camp. When she was released from the camp she could not sleep." Can you see it? These are the sentences which are underlined. So I assume those are the symptoms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Excuse the interruption, Your Honour. I'm just wondering if again we might be straying into areas that are referring to matters that were in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we're going into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Private session, Mr. Registrar

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
